speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ask for leave to move, seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver South (Mr. Green) the adjournment of the house for the purpose of discussing a definite matter of urgent public importance, namely, the written submissions made by the government of Canada to the special deputies of the council of foreign ministers on the proposed peace treaties with Germany and Austria and the Canadian position taken with respect to a full participation of this country in the making of these treaties.
The urgency element in this motion will be recognized at once in view of the fact that the foreign ministers are scheduled to meet in Moscow in ten days. Unless full opportunity of debate is provided now, the, Moscow meeting may be over before the views of the Canadian people as expressed by parliament are known to them and to the world. This should not be.
The debate on the address, which resumes next Monday, will afford a wholly inadequate opportunity for parliament as a whole to make its voice heard on these matters and these alone. This further contributes to the urgency surrounding this motion now.
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs): May I be allowed to make a suggestion with respect to this motion? There is no doubt that its subject matter is one of great importance and interest to the Canadian people, and that there is some urgency in view of the fact that the meeting of foreign ministers is to take place in Moscow within ten days. However, at this time we are dealing with emergency legislation, and under the motion adopted by the house this is the last day that that emergency legislation can be dealt with until the address has been disposed of.
If the hon. member would care to hold his motion until Monday I would not venture to suggest there could be any opposition to the motion, although there are other matters of urgent importance; it would be within the jurisdiction of the house to decide which should have priority. Standing order 31 provides for the manner in which that is deter-

mined. Even if there were opposition to the hon. member's motion on Monday, and twenty members were to stand, the hon. member would have leave to discuss it. subtopic: PROTECTION OF WATERSHED EAST OF ROCKIES TO HUDSON BAT-AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: PROTECTION OF WATERSHED EAST OF ROCKIES TO HUDSON BAT-AGREEMENT WITH ALBERTA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make which I think should be made first to the house.
As the members of the house know, the government has been carrying on negotiations with the province of Alberta for the adequate protection of the forests on that part of the east slope of the Rocky mountains forming the watershed of the rivers arising therein and flowing eastward through the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, and finally draining into Hudson bay. The importance of forest cover to stream flow regulation has long been recognized and need not be emphasized.
The dominion is protecting that part of the watershed which lies within the boundaries of Jasper, Banff and Waterton lakes national parks. It will be recalled that all the natural resources, including the administration of forests, was transferred to the western provinces in 1930. As a result, from that date the responsibility for protecting the watershed lying outside the boundaries of the national parks was placed upon the province of Alberta. The government of that province has frankly admitted its inability adequately to protect the area and took the view that the expenditures it was making were all that could be justified in the interest of the province alone and that the problem was of vital concern not only to the provinces of Saskatchewan and Manitoba, but to the whole of Canada.
I think everyone will agree that the protection of this most important watershed is a national problem and that it would be against the national interest if the responsibility therefor were left solely to Alberta.
It has not been an easy problem to solve. The area is large and comprises approximately 6,300,000 acres. The question of the other resources had to be considered. The province was unwilling to give up the administration of them. However, I am pleased to report that as a result of extensive discussions during the past year with Premier Manning and the Hon. Mr. Tanner, minister of lands and mines, we have been successful in arriving at the outline of an agreement which will be submitted concurrently for the consideration of this parliament and of the provincial legislature.
Briefly, the proposed agreement provides for the establishment of a board to plan, direct and supervise the construction, operation and maintenance of all projects and facilities
required for the proper protection and conservation of the area with a view to obtaining and maintaining the greatest possible flow of water from the Saskatchewan river and its tributaries. The board will consist of three members, two, including the chairman, to be appointed by the dominion, and the other member to be appointed by the province.
The dominion agrees to make available to the board a sum not exceeding $6,300,000 during the first six years of the agreement for the capital expenditures required for the construction of forest improvements, the making of a forest inventory, for reforestation purposes and such other works and services as the board may consider necessary. Further, the dominion will provide for the yearly maintenance of a complete protective and forest management service and for research in silviculture and scientific services, an amount which with the provincial contribution will enable the board to spend annually a sum up to $300,000.
The province agrees to contribute annually towards the maintenance costs the sum of $125,000 or fifty per cent of the maintenance costs if the amount thereof in any year should be less than $250,000. The province retains the revenue derived from the area provided that if it should exceed the amount of the province's contribution then to the extent of the excess will the latter be increased. The province also agrees to share equally in the cost of fighting any large or extraordinary fires. The province will act as agent for the board in carrying out the necessary works, subject to the conditions provided for in the agreement.
The term of the agreement is for a definite period of twenty-five years and will continue from year to year thereafter subject to termination by either party upon giving one year's notice.
I am sure all the members will welcome the announcement I have just made. We who are living today may not derive many actual benefits from this conservation project, but we would be very remiss in discharging our responsibilities if we failed to consider the interests and welfare of those who follow us. In conclusion, may I add a word of appreciation of the wholehearted cooperation extended by Premier Manning and the Hon. Mr. Tanner in working out the details of the arrangement. In our discussions at no time did they forget the wider interests involved.

The house resumed from Thursday, February 27, consideration in committee of Bill No. 23, to amend the Canadian Wheat Board Act, 1935-Mr. MacKinnon-Mr. Golding in the chair.
On section 5 (section 17)-Powers of administration of the board.

I should like to remind hon. members that before the committee adjourned last night the Minister of Justice moved an amendment which would remove subsection 2 of section 17 from the bill. The committee was discussing the amendment when we adjourned last night. I think the committee had better decide whether the subsection is to remain or whether it is to be removed in accordance with the amendment moved by the minister.

Before the committee
adjourned last night the Minister of Agriculture was making a statement with regard to the deletion of this subsection. He argued that the subsection might very well be deleted because there was protection given to the farmers in that the government through the board must take deliverv of grain.
The minister said, as quoted at page 884 of Hansard:
All it says is that if a farmer delivers wheat to an elevator we must buy it and the wheat board must take delivery of the wheat.
Mr. Queleh:	If there is room.
Mr. Gardiner:	Yes, if it is delivered there
and there is room, they must take it.
Earlier in the debate the Minister of Justice suggested an amendment to subsection 1 of section 17. The amendment was not passed, but its effect was that the board may, notwithstanding anything contained in the Canada Grain Act, but subject to directions, if any, contained in any order, by order prescribe certain things. Among the things included are deliveries of grain. I contend that if the amendment suggested by the Minister of Justice were to pass making this the master act, it could override the Canada Grain Act. If that is so, the argument of the Minister of Agriculture is unsound. If the amendment were to pass the board would not of necessity have to take delivery of grain at all, because it would override section 108 of the Canada Grain Act, which states:
The operator or manager of every licensed public country elevator shall, at all reasonable hours on each day upon which the elevator is

Canadian Wheat Board Act
open, receive all grain offered thereat for storage without discrimination and in the order in which it is offered, provided that there is in the elevator available storage accommodation for grain of the variety and grade of such grain and of the character desired by the person by whom the grain is offered.
(3) Any breach of the provisions of this section shall be punishable on summary conviction by imprisonment for not more than six months or by a fine not exceeding five hundred dollars.
If we delete this subsection, then the other amendment, which would make this the master act overriding the Canada Grain Act, should not be passed.
The committee is dealing with subsection 2 of section 17 on page 9.

That is exactly what I am discussing. I am discussing the effect on subsection 2 of the amendment suggested by the Minister of Justice. I am convinced that if we delete the subsection it will mean that the board will not of necessity have to take delivery of grain. They will be able to decide the amount of grain that they are prepared to accept. They will be able to accept ten bushels, whereas this subsection speaks of a minimum of fourteen bushels. Unless the minister can offer a much better argument than has so far been advanced, or unless it is stated in section 21, that the board will take delivery of all grain grown up to and including the 1949 crop, whether that grain has been delivered on July SI, 1950 or not; and if it is offered at a later date and has been held back on the farm because of lack of storage in the elevator facilities of the country, they should then take delivery of it under the price agreed to under the 1945-50 food contract.
I should like to have a definite statement from the minister. The member for Acadia tried his best to get a statement; I tried, the member for Mackenzie tried, but we have not been able to get any statement from any of the three ministers as to what will be the position of the farmer with grain left on his farm because there are no facilities to deliver it on July 31, 1949. It is a very simple point, and there should not be any quibbling about it.
The Minister of Agriculture spoke for several minutes last night trying, as I thought, to draw red herrings across the trail and get the committee's attention away from that point. But so far as we are concerned, we want a statement on that point before we are prepared to see the clause deleted.

Yesterday it was suggested by the Minister of Agriculture, and by other members as well, that we would make better progress if we allowed this section to stand until we had discussed section 21, because the question in all our minds is, what will the government do in regard to deliveries. Will they take delivery of all wheat? The Minister of Agriculture suggested that that question is answered in section 21. I suggest to the minister that we allow this section to stand until we have taken up section 21 so that we may have the whole matter clarified.

I should like to clear up what seems to be in the minds of hon. members opposite. It was not this side that asked to have subsection 2 taken out. It was members on the other side. We do not care whether it is taken out or left in.
We never asked that it be taken out.

Individuals may say so, but the statement was made, and it appears in Hansard, by two or three different members that they would not permit this bill to be given second reading until they had a declaration on the question whether it was to be left in or taken out. The minister got up yesterday when the house opened and said that we were prepared to take it out. Well, we are prepared to leave it in. We put it in in the first place, and I do not see why there should be any argument about it. We will do whatever members opposite want to have done. Personally I do not think it makes much difference whether it is in or out.

I think there has been a misunderstanding. When the member for Acadia spoke the other day in reference to section 17, subsection 2, he pointed out that there was a possibility that the government might not take more than fourteen bushels, but what he was definitely trying to convey to the minister and to the government and the house was that under that section the government need not take any more. But his point was that the government should declare itself clearly whether or not it was prepared to take all the wheat produced and offered for sale in that contract period. The Minister of Agriculture said that in his opinion that section had no bearing on that point but that section 20 was the one under which it should be dealt with, and it is my recollection that the Minister of Agriculture then suggested that we leave section 17 and

Canadian Wheat Board Act

go on to section 20 where that question could be discussed. If that is true, and if the Minister of Agriculture can convince the members that the question is well taken care of under section 20, then there should be no difficulty about section 17. But until he can do that, I think there will be considerable doubt in the minds of hon. members, and therefore I suggest to the member for Acadia and the Minister of Agriculture that we pass on to section 20 and dispose of that, so as to find out where we stand, and then come back to section 17.
There is no objection to that procedure. Let 17 stand and we can take 18, 19, 20 and 21, and after that we can come back to this question.
May I quote from Hansard to prove that we did not ask that it be taken out.
It does not matter, anyway.

At page 744 of Hansard I made this statement:
Let me say to the minister that, before we can support the second reading of this bill, we must have assurance that when we reach the committee stage he will either move an amendment or accept an amendment to commit the government to accepting all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950.
Then at page 747:
We are satisfied that in order to build up the prosperity of the nation, and the prosperity of the grain grower under this agreement, it will be necessary to have an amendment to subsection 2 of section 17 definitely committing the government to the acceptance of all wheat produced and offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950.
There was no suggestion of withdrawing the section; it was a question of amending it.
You were not the only speaker.

An hour before we
adjourned last night I suggested that we let this section stand.
Then let us do it.

Will somebody make up his mind?
Section stands.
_ Cn section 5 (section 18)-Inquiries and investigation to ascertain facilities.

This clause provides for inquiries under the Inquiries Act, giving the members of the board the same powers as commissioners under that act. The commis-

sioners under the Inquiries Act have very large powers. This was in the former act too. Has this section in the former act been untilized at all?
No; it has not been used.

Section agreed to.
Section 5 (section 19) agreed to.
On section 5 (section 20)-"Pool period" defined.

This is the section that was referred to when we were discussing section 17, and the point I was making at that time is this. Section 20 reads:
Subject to section twenty-six of this act, in this part "pool period" means
(a)	each crop year prior to the first day of August, nineteen hundred and forty-five;
(b)	the period commencing on the said first day of August and ending on the thirty-first day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty;
These two periods are definitely determined. The first is all the period up to July 31, 1945, and the second is the five-year period, four years of which are covered by the British contract down to July 31, 1950. The next clause (c) states that this matter is to be brought back to parliament before the end of the second period in order to determine what we are going to do after July 31, 1950. In other words, in reference to the matters referred to, this act will be brought back into the house prior to 1950. Last night we were discussing what the condition would be in July, 1950. We shall be in a much better position to know what the condition is going to be in the last session prior to July 31, 1950, than we can possibly be now, and the provision put in here is to see that the bill does come back in order to determine what we shall do from there on. It is to take care of such matters as we discussed last evening. In other words, if this bill and the British agreement work out to the satisfaction of the majority of the members of this house, then I have no doubt the house will simply say we shall go right on as we are.
If a new contract were made with Britain or an international arrangement were made in the meantime on a multilateral basis, we would simply be saying that that contract was extended over a certain period of time; and if in saying that we say that the initial payment is still $1.35 a bushel, there is nothing else at all which needs to be said. It is just the same at the end of 1950 as it was at the end of 1945-46. 1946-47 and 1947-48. We are just going on in a period during which pool-

Canadian Wheat Board Act
ing is being carried on; and if there is no change whatsoever in the initial payment, then we are not concerned whether there is still wheat on the farm, in the elevators, or anywhere else. We are just going on into another period when there is an initial payment of $1.35, and we get our participation paid up to that date. Whatever participation is earned over the next period, whether it is one, two or three years, will be provided1 for in the legislation at that time.
There are conditions which could arise, some of which have been discussed by hon. members who fear that the rights of the farmers may not be properly protected. It is said that there may be a big crop in 1950, that there may be a surplus of grain. If there is a big crop and a surplus of grain, and the initial payment is still to be $1.35, it will not make any difference. If there is a big crop and if the results of this contract and of this period show that an initial payment of SI.40 or $1.45 can be paid, then if I know the farmers of western Canada I do not think many of them will want to deliver their wheat; they will want to hold it over to get, not $1.35 but $1.40 or $1.45. Under those circumstances, this house may want to do something with regard to that. I would imagine what they would want to do would be to say that immediately they had determined that the initial payment is to be raised, on that very day the payment would have to go up. They probably would not wait even until the end of July to do it, because if they did they would not get delivery of any grain in the meantime.

What about the other
side?

Let us come to the other side. Suppose it has to go down. Unless there is a shortage of storage space, every farmer in the country will get all his crop in before the end of July. He will see to it that it is in if the initial payment is going down to $1.25 and it is $1.35 up to the end of July. Every farmer will rush his crop into the elevator.
If there is space.

Yes, if there is space. On the question whether there will be space, may I say, first, that there have been twelve months in which to deliver it, and, second, that we did during the war add approximately 150 million bushels of storage space to the elevator system of this country-but not because we needed it before the war. We had too much elevator space before the war for
the needs of Canada in times of peace. But during the war when we had to pile up 600 million bushels of grain in our elevators and on our farms and then provide for a new crop, we had to put storage not only on our farms but at almost every delivery point in western Canada. We had to put extra storage at Fort William. I understand that the extra storage there has been largely pulled down; it was temporary. But those of us who live on the prairies know that the special storage put up in our own towns and villages is still there.
Oh, no.

Well, the greater part of it is still there, although there may be the odd place where it has been pulled, down. I do not know where my hon. friends live, but I travel over more of the west, I think, than any other member of the House of Commons and I still maintain that storage is there in most places. The figure I received the other day is to the effect that some 95 million bushels of it is still in existence, which brings us up to well over 500 million bushels of available storage. Unless we are going to grow the biggest crop we ever grew, on the biggest acreage we ever had, I do not think there is any possibility at any time during the next four or five years of our having a shortage of storage space. There may be individual points at which the elevators are jammed, although there is not a shortage of space generally, and something may have to be done about situations of that kind.
Although the wheat board have sometimes found difficulty in doing things as quickly as some people would like to have them done, in the end they have not found any difficulty in meeting special conditions of the kind. Where only a small proportion of the farmers are involved, ways and means can be found of taking care of the situation. But I do not see any possibility, under the conditions which are likely to exist, of such a situation developing. But even if it did develop, when will this house be in a better position to deal with it than when they know it has developed and when they are sitting here in 1950 dealing with the situation? We can sit here for days and discuss all the possible things which could develop, and try to cover them in this bill; but I am sure when we were through, after we had gone home, the ordinary farmer would think of many things we had forgotten about which might have been put in the bill if an attempt were to be made to protect everybody against everything that might happen.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

I suggest that this matter has been discussed widely with those who are most concerned with it and who are dealing with it every day, and they and the government think that the matter is safeguarded/ in every way in which it can possibly be safeguarded without putting into the bill outlines of a situation which in all probability will never develop but which no one can say definitely will not arise. We have put a provision into the bill which makes it certain that the legislation will come before the house again before 1950, and at that time this possible situation can be dealt with in the light of the knowledge then available.

We are dealing with section 20, which defines "pool period". This is the section which provides that from now on the pool period shall be a five-year period rather than a period of single years as in the past. With that policy on the part of the government we are not in agreement. We think the pool period should be the period of the crop year, and that whatever money has been collected in sales by the government in addition to what it has paid out should be paid out on the participation certificates each year. The section reads as follows:
Subject to section twenty-six of this act, in this part "pool period" means-
There are three subsections, (a), (b) and
(c); I shall refer only to the one I am dealing with, which reads:
(b) the period commencing on the first day of August-
Meaning the first day of August, 1945.

and ending on the thirty-first day of July, nineteen hundred and fifty.
This means that the five-year period we are now in is to be regarded as a pool period. During that year the board is to advance the amount of $1.35 a bushel each year, but no more until the end, and at the end of the period whatever may be left in the pool will be paid out. We think these balances should be paid out at the conclusion of each crop year. I therefore move:
That paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of section 20 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Any crop year prior to or subsequent to the first day of August, 1945."
In simple language this means that the pool period would become a one-year period rather than a five-year period. In connection with this amendment I should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce, or perhaps the former minister of finance or the present Minister of Finance, to tell us how much money the board is holding in connection with the 1943 crop, the 1944 crop and the 1945 crop, and also what rate of interest any such moneys

may be earning. It is a fact that as long as the board or the government holds this money, and it can only invest it at a relatively low rate of interest, probably Jess than three per cent. The owners of that money, the farmers, are denied the use of it to pay off their obligations on which they are charged up to six and seven per cent interest. The point of this amendment is to make the pool period one year rather than five years.

I should like to have the opinion of those who may be speaking in regard to an increased expenditure on the part of the government as a result of this amendment. I am of the opinion that it would be out of order on that ground, but I should like to hear an expression of opinion by hon. members.

Well, Mr. Chairman, it will be recognized by everyone in the committee that no one on this side is allowed to make any amendment that would have the effect of bringing about increased expenditure on the part of the government. But this amendment does not do anything of the kind. Here are the facts, and the committee may consider them. The government, through its agency, the wheat board, takes possession of the farmers' wheat. It sells that wheat and gives the farmer part of the money received, and holds the balance. All we are asking is that the board pay the farmer the balance of the money each year rather than after five years. That would make no charge on the treasury. This is the money of the farmers; it is not the money of the taxpayers. So the point of order you raised, Mr. Chairman, I suggest has no relevancy in this connection.

I do not see that this amendment would involve an increased expenditure by the government, but it would destroy a principle contained in this act for which organized agriculture has been working over a number of years; that is, stability in the price of grain for a period of years. If the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition were to be adopted it might mean that this year we would obtain quite a high price. We do not know what the price might be next year, and we know even less about what it might be the year after. The amendment would remove the basis of stability which at present exists under the act. I am in favour of annual payments on participation certificates, but we maintain that the only way this can be done and at the same time maintain stability is to make those payments on the basis of a parity price, which would not fluctuate. Parity in this country would not fluctuate to the extent that world prices might

Canadian Wheat Board Act
fluctuate over a five-year period. Therefore we would get the result we desire by making the participation certificates payable yearly on the basis of a parity price. In that way we can maintain the stability feature of the act and at the same time give the full benefit to the farmer. I think by his amendment the leader of the opposition is defeating the purpose of the farmers in connection with stability.

I wish to concur in the statement made already, that payments made in * accordance with this amendment would not be increased by expenditures by the crown, because they would be money really belonging to the farmers. But that is as far as I am prepared to go at the moment with the leader of the opposition. My colleague the hon. member for Melfort has just pointed out that there is a way by which the farmers could receive payment of their participation certificates each year, by way of an equalization or parity payment. From what we have seen so far, however, I doubt whether the government would be willing to do that. If the government do not care to adopt that suggestion, then in all sincerity I submit to the leader of the opposition that instead of destroying one of the main principles of the bill our purpose can be achieved in another way. That is, when the board has considerable funds on band, interim payments might be made. I believe a majority of the farmers would be satisfied with that. I made some reference to this yesterday. If the board has millions of dollars on hand it will find it necessary to invest that money in other securities. The pool period is fairly well advanced now, and after another year the board will be in possession of a very considerable amount of money that really belongs to the producers. Then they could go to work and make an interim payment, still retaining a reasonable amount on hand to help level off the balance of the pool period.

The farmers of western Canada have been crying for a stabilized market for a number of years, and under the government plan as outlined in this bill we will have that stabilized market. Let us say that wheat is $1.20 this year, $1.40 next year, $1.60 the year after that. $1.70 the following year, and that the following year it drops to $1.10 or $1. So far as I can see this is the only way you can have a stabilized market over a five-year period. The farmers of western Canada are not concerned about the government holding a few dollars, but they are concerned about seeing that the conditions of
1930 to 1935 do not return. If the government has a few dollars that have accumulated over a period of years I do not think there will be any objection.

The leader of the opposition recognizes that all the expenses of the wheat board are to be paid out of the sale of the wheat of the producer, but this five-year pooling is retroactive legislation, something which I have heard the Minister of Justice object to on the floor of this house on more than one occasion. I think the agreement with Great Britain came into force after the commencement of this crop year 1946-47, yet according to this pooling basis the proceeds from the sales of the 1945^46 crop year are being put into the pool. The proceeds from that crop year should have been disposed of before the United Kingdom-Canada wheat agreement came into force. However, it is proposed to put the proceeds from that year's business into the five-year pool.
The leader of the opposition has asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce a definite question, as to how much money the wheat board had left at the end of 1943; how much it had left at the end of 1944, which year has all been cleaned up, and how much was left at the end of 1945-46, which is the first year they propose to include in the five-year pool. The operations for that year were completed before the operation of the agreement with the United Kingdom commenced.
I do not think it is good business to create a five-year pool on that basis. This money was obtained from the efforts of the producers and it should be disbursed annually. People talk about organized agriculture, but I am sure if you consulted the wheat pools of Canada you would get the request for the disbursement of these profits annually. They want an early settlement whenever the payments can be figured out and the cheques issued. The producers want to work on an annual basis.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Unless the interests of what I call the taxpayers are to be disregarded almost entirely, then the figure of $1.35 would have to be quite a different figure if we were going to pay out annually. There would be no guaranteed $1.35 for two years from now or three years from now. There could not possibly be, because the risk of very great loss would be so enormous.

We have listened to the Minister of Justice tell us that the price that the farmer is to get must be the average of what he can sell for on the export market. Under the British agreement for two years they will get $1.55; for one year they may get only $1.25 and for the last year only SI. The minister says because of that they can make a payment of $1.35, and that is all they can pay. I want to ask this government whether it stands for a fair price for the farmer or whether the price is to be the average of what it sells its wheat for outside? In three years from now the price of wheat may be $1 per bushel, and they may find that the best international agreement they can make will be for $1 or $1.25 per bushel. Is the government then going to pay the farmer as little as that?
If it is, where is the stability in its policy, and at what a level that stability will be! Does the government stand for a fair price to the farmer for his wheat, or does it not? With costs as they are, under these conditions $1.35 is not a fair price.

The question which the leader of the opposition has raised is an important one when associated with this legislation, but it brings us right back to the point raised by the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Humboldt. It strikes at the principle underlying the legislation. The principle underlying the legislation is to give the farmer a stabilized return, and as high a stabilized return as it is possible to give him over a long period without endangering his own position in relation to the other taxpayers of this country.
As was said on the second reading of the bill, it is much better and more in the interests of the farmer to have a price which can be assured to him out of the trading of his own product than to have him dependent upon a price which must rely upon the taxation of two-thirds of the population which does not grow farm products for the existence of the policy. We have had enough experience with that kind of thing to know that 
when you get to charging the taxpayers too much, the taxpayers vote that kind of policy out of existence. This legislation makes provision for the building up of a plan under which the farmer knows what minimum he is going to receive for his product over a long period.
The question involved in the discussion taking place is whether this is properly a four-year term or a five-year term. That is the first question that is raised in connection with whether payments ought to be made for the 1945 crop year irrespective of whether we have annual payments or not.

The bill provides for a
five year term.

The bill provides for a
five year term, but that is the question in the minds of the people who are discussing it. For example, we had before us today the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and they made strong recommendations to the effect that the participation for the 1945 crop ought to be paid out. That is the only representation that has been made by the farm organizations in connection with payments on a yearly basis. They contended that the participation payments for 1945 should neyer have been taken into the pool, that they should have been paid out at the beginning of this present crop year.
In reply to that I would say that the discussion with regard to this policy began on the floor of this house, I think in September, 1945. At the beginning of that crop year, when the farmers were harvesting their 1945 crop, the suggestion was made that we ought to follow the price up. The price had passed $1.55 per bushel on the way up and it was said by some people that we should take off all controls on the price of wheat and let our price follow the American price up as high as it was going to go. Eventually, of course, we would follow it down.
Look the other way when you say that.

I wanted my hon.
friend to hear it and understand it. They suggested that we follow the price right up, but the government said that that would not be the proper thing to do. We have been discussing this matter before the international wheat committee ever since 1922. The question whether or not we could get multilateral agreements on wheat was first discussed at the end of the first war in Rome. That organization was moved from Rome to London, and then from London to Washington. It did not make any difference where its

Canadian Wheat Board Act
headquarters were, they were never able to arrive at a conclusion with regard to it. Any conclusions they did arrive at were departed from shortly afterward by someone, and therefore they were not carried into practice.
In 1945 the committee met in London. It had gone back to London from Washington. Before the government took any action in the matter they sent a cable to London and asked for a decision on the question that had been before that committee for some time. The question had been submitted by the representatives of this government. There had been a discussion on acreage control and quota control of wheat delivered by the different countries into the markets of the world, and a discussion on price. There had been an agreement reached on quota control. Canada was to have 40 per cent of the world's market in wheat, as was stated here the other day in the submission to the committee. It was agreed years ago that Canada was to get 40 per cent of the world's market in wheat, that she should market each year 40 per cent of the wheat delivered into the markets of the world. In addition it was agreed years ago what the acreage control should be. In the last arrangement it was agreed that what we had done in 1941, when we paid the farmers S4 an acre to take land out of wheat and put it in summer-fallow, was sufficient action by Canada in acreage control to warrant the international committee in accepting what we had done as being all that could be asked of Canada. So those two questions had been agreed upon-acreage control and quota control. The one question there had not been agreement upon was the question of price.
At one time it was agreed that the price for a period after the war was to have been the price that was realized by Canada in making her last sale to Great Britain prior to the end of the war. That was in 1942. In 1943, for reasons which have often been explained to the house, we suspended operations on the Winnipeg grain exchange; therefore there could be no price established in Winnipeg for grain in the last transaction between this country and Great Britain after that date. As a result that provision in the agreement was of no effect. Bo there was no price agreement. We had an actual agreement in 1942 on acreage, quotas and price, but when that action was taken in 1943, the price arrangement was no longer effective. A number of meetings and discussions took place as to what the price arrangement should be. The last submission made by Canada prior to 83166-57
September of 1945 was that the price should vary between $1 and $1.50 a bushel. That was discussed by the committee on two or three occasions, but agreement had not been reached. So in August or September of 1945 we sent a cable to London asking the committee for a decision on the question in order that we might decide whether we should follow wheat up beyond $1.55 or conform with the wishes of the international committee. We got a cable back saying they could not reach agreement.
A day or two after we got that cable the Minister of Trade and Commerce came into this house and said that the Canadian government was prepared to do what we had suggested to the international committee might be done as an international arrangement, that we were prepared to guarantee to the farmers of Canada a minimum price of $1 for five years beginning with the crop of 1945, and that we were prepared to go on selling wheat for the time being at $1.55. We said that we would deliver wheat only to our overseas allies at that price; that if the people of the United States or any country which was not our ally in the war desired to buy Canadian wheat they would have to pay the world price for it or the price that had been established on the Chicago grain exchange. So as regards wheat sold to the United States for feed, and we sold approximately 160,000,000 bushels in 1943 and 1944-the United States has an embargo against our wheat being used in the United States for food-that wheat went to the United States at the American price less the duty that has to be paid under any circumstances to get wheat into the United States.
What is the United States duty on wheat?

It has been 42 cents a bushel ever since 1930. They will not admit into their countiy more than 800,000 bushels of wheat a year for human consumption in the United States. So there is no way of selling wheat into the United States at the American price. There has been an embargo against it, I am told, ever since 1938.
With that situation existing we said: The government of Canada is going to go on selling wheat to Britain and our other allies overseas at $1.55 a bushel, but to anyone else we are going to sell at the world price, but we will guarantee that no matter what the world price of wheat is, the floor price for five years will be $1 a bushel. That is the situation which existed at the beginning

of the 1945 crop. That was a five-year plan, a five-year arrangement, and mo one ever discussed it from any other point of view, either with the British government or with any other government, or with the farm organizations; and no one ever suggested that it ought to be anything else but a five-year programme.
Now I come down to the last week before the British agreement was signed, when we knew all the facts with regard to it. The Minister of Trade and Commerce and I met-
I have stated this in the pool board meetings in western Canada and I have their consent to state it anywhere-we met the representatives of all the farmers' grain handling organizations in western Canada-the Saskatchewan wheat pool, the Manitoba wheat pool, the Alberta wheat pool, the United Grain Growers. These organizations were all present, together with the president and secretary of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, and a representative of the wheat growers of Ontario. The meeting was held for the purpose of discussing what the initial payment ought to be following this agreement. We were in a position at that time to inform them what that British agreement was, because it had all been agreed to. The agreement was signed I think two days later.
What was the date of that meeting?

It was some time last summer-I think in July. The first question I asked the representatives of the farm organizations when we settled down was this. I said: Am I right in believing that the highest initial payment that has been asked for officially by the farm organizations is $1.25 a bushel? Without any exception they said yes. The next question I asked was: Am I right in believing that the farmers would like to have a price which might be termed parity? The answer to that was yes. Beyond that I do not know that I had their consent to this, but in all the previous meetings it had been agreed that parity based upon the price which had been received for wheat from 1926 to 1929 was $1.41 a bushel. Therefore I said: Am I right in believing that you now would like to have an initial payment of about $1.40 a bushel in order that it may be somewhere near the parity price as it has been calculated? And they said yes. As a matter of fact, Mr. Chairman, they then submitted arguments as to why the advance payment ought to be $1.40.
I tell this story in order to show that the first time anyone ever suggested that participation be paid on the 1945 crop was during
	* _ :	|
that discussion. It was not suggested by the farm organizations; it was suggested by myself, and every one of the farm organizations will agree that that is so. Why was it suggested? When the proposal was made that we should start off with $1.40, the argument was used which I have twice used in the committee, namely, is it not much better for the farmer to be in a position to say that whatever price he is getting, he is getting it for his own wheat, paid for by the people of Canada, paid for by the British or anyone else who wants to buy it? It is better that way if we can arrange it, and everyone, I think, was agreeable to that.
The next thing was to calculate how much could be paid without any fear of loss. It was suggested that $1.35 was the highest price that could be paid without any fear of loss, on the calculating that had been done by those who look after matters of the kind for the government. Others checked it and it was agreed that that was as high as one could go if all the crop years were taken into consideration.
Then the suggestion was made that since we could not pay more than $1.35 over the whole five years without involving someone other than the farmers themselves, probably we could develop a plan based on four years and pay the participation on the first year at the end of the year 1945. We asked the definite question whether it would be more satisfactory to the farmers if we paid the participation on the 1945 crop and then paid $1.35 through for the four years. The representatives of the farm organization said that would be more satisfactory to them. It was not their proposal; it was our suggestion to them.
A few days following that they held a meeting in Winnipeg and submitted the question to that meeting. It was discussed behind closed doors by the representatives of the farm organizations. We continued to make our calculations and finally had to come back and say that after calculating the matter as we had done previously it would be impossible to maintain the floor at $1.36; we would have to come down to a lower floor in order to maintain the position that we had taken previously, if we had paid the 1945 participation and put it on a four-year basis. Therefore the question would have to be discussed again from the point of view of the five-year period.
Representatives of the farm organizations flew from Ottawa to Winnipeg to complete the discussion in Winnipeg and finally received the agreement of the organizations under some protests that it would be satisfactory to proceed on that basis. Hon. members know what

results from discussions of that kind. When discussions of that kind are started-and we assumed the responsibility for starting them, not the farm organizations-it is not easy to stop them, particularly when you start them in that way. These matters have been discussed in farm organizations ever since. Farm organizations have been passing resolutions about it here and there. But the heads of the organizations know what the discussions were which took place and the reason for them. They know what was involved in them, and when they come to talk to us they are not talking of this year-by-year proposal of the leader of the opposition. In the statement they made to us today they asked for payment of the 1945 participation, thereby going back to the suggestion which was made to them by us last summer. They suggest that that ought to be paid.
The leader of the opposition says that parity now is 11.55, therefore we ought to pay $1.55 to the farmer. Two years ago somebody agreed that it was $1.41. They were not so sure about it a year ago. I have no doubt that if all this calamity takes place which has been suggested since the discussion started, by 1950 somebody will be saying that it is $1, not $1.55. But I do not think the calamity will take place. One of my reasons for saying that is that I believe the long-time contract, especially with a nation like Britain, will give stability to our agriculture over a five-year period such as it has never had before. Believing that, I do not think that parity will come down to $1 in that period of time, but it can come down to $1.35 or $1.30. All we are suggesting is that the farmers should have parity, but not parity of today or parity of yesterday. They ought to have a parity based upon a period of five years, and that ought to be paid to them.
The hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Humboldt have ideas of their own as to what might be done about that. They think that we might calculate that parity every year and that we might pay out the difference between $1.35 and whatever that parity is in each year as we go along. I do not know just where parity will go. I do not know that I know exactly how to calculate it myself. I have to take someone's word for it and perhaps check on it.
It can be done.
It can be done, but I think it will be agreed by everyone that to keep the matter right you have to do it at least every week.

Once a year.

I doubt whether we can get very much by calculating it weekly, monthly or annually, if what you want is long-time stability. We believe that farmers do want long-time stability, and that it ought to be for a period of five years. Therefore this legislation is based on that idea.
I may say something which perhaps the government would not follow me in all the way, but which I think any government which is here at the time will have to follow, and that is that if the situation develops where this government is to have an enormous sum of money piled up, somebody will insist on our paying it out. I do not believe this government or any other government will be permitted to pile up and hold in the treasury, let us say, $300 or $400 million which belongs to somebody else.
How much money have you piled up now?
It is not known exactly what it is, and I do not think I should make any guess at it.
It should be quite a bit.

Yes. But everyone knows that you can lose quite a bit of money in the wheat business in a short time. For example in western Canada we had pools which handled wheat, and every member who was associated with the wheat pools will tell you this. The chief mistake that was made was making too high an initial payment and finding a little later on that those who agreed to their establishing that high initial payment would not let them put it down when they came to the meetings from time to time. I can understand people who do not believe in this principle, who do not believe in this legislation at all, trying to get us on to such a high basis in connection with initial payments that in the end we shall be defeated in exactly the same way as the wheat pools were. Believing that, Mr. Chairman, I do not think this committee should try to lead, not the government of Canada but the farmers into a position where they set up in this country an organization for the marketing of their wheat which runs any risk within the next four years of having to make an appeal to the people of Canada to pay out of the treasury money to take care of losses.
If we have to do that I know what will happen when parliament meets in 1950 to consider what we shall do after 1950. There is only one sure way of having legislation brought down here in 1950 which will continue

marketing under the pooling system and marketing under long-term contracts, and that is to be able to say in 1950 that no one took any loss whatsoever in it, that the farmer got his $1.35, that no one had to pay anything to help him get it except the people who ate his food, and that at the end of it we can say to all the other people in Canada-because you must remember that there are only about 280,000 of us, that is to say, heads of families, who are growing wheat: We have asked the government of Canada to do a job that will make it possible for us to market our product to better advantage than we have ever marketed it before. The government of Canada has done that. We have tried it out for five years and now we have proved to you that it does not cost anyone else a red cent; and that being the case, we think the government of Canada, or rather the parliament of Canada, ought to continue the system.
Unless we can do that at the end of the five-year period, we have not much chance of having the system continued, and so I say that the member for Melfort and the member for Humboldt were one hundred per cent right when they said that the motion made to the committee by the leader of the opposition strikes at the very principle underlying the whole plan that is contained in the bill. I suggest therefore that the committee ought to vote the proposal down.
On the question whether the motion is in order, I think there is much to be said in favour of its being in order; that is to say, we are dealing with the farmers' money. I hope it will not result in our dealing with anyone else's money. If we were to do what my hon, friend suggests we should do, probably there might be an argument in that direction. But as the bill is drawn, as the section is drawn, it is intended to safeguard us against that kind of thing and I think it does. Therefore I do not think that any of the ministers who are interested' in the bill, or the government, will urge any particular line of action on the chairman. He is in charge of the committee and will give whatever ruling he thinks is the right one, but we are not asking for a ruling that the motion is out of order. We simply say that we believe the question ought to be decided on its merits, and1 can be decided on its merits, and if it is we will decide in favour of the principle, which is long-term stabilization of farm prices over a period of five years.

When I was speaking the Minister of Justice asked me if I believed in floor prices or an initial payment, which I 
certainly do, and at that time someone else took up the discussion and I did not have an opportunity to finish.

If the hon. member will wait a moment I will allow him to speak. I have listened to the discussion, and as I pointed out before, what I am concerned about is as to whether the motion will involve expenditure on the part of the government, and what effect the amendment would have on the operating clause, 22, of the bill and on subsection 3 of 5, on page 4, that is to say:
Losses, if any, sustained by the board
(a)	from its operations under part 111 of this act in relation to any pool period fixed thereunder, during such period, or
(b)	from its other operations under this act during any crop year.
That is what I am concerned about. If I have the assurance that the motion will not involve additional expenditure and is not likely to, then I will not rule against it.
The chairman has not ruled it out of order.
Not yet.

In that case I should like to finish my remarks in answer to the Minister of Justice. It will be recalled that he was Minister of Finance throughout the war years, and under his policy, and the policy of Mr. Donald Gordon, of price stabilization, you will realize that these same wheat producers in three years made a contribution amounting to $394,000,000 odd in order to help out that stabilization policy, over and above their share of taxation which they bore in common with every other taxpayer in the country. The statistics will prove that. This is interesting now, in view of the statements made by the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture outside this house, and since the termination of the war, that owing to the great contribution the farmers had made not only in wheat but in agricultural production generally in order to maintain price stabilization in Canada, that point would certainly have to be taken into consideration during the post-war period by the government of the day. Both the Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture have spoken in those terms outside this house on more occasions than one. As I say, these same wheat producers have made a contribution of $394,000,000. The last report tabled by the price stabilization board the other day showed an expenditure of approximately $400,000,000 to date since 1941.

Order. I do not believe we should get into a discussion on lumber or any of these other commodities. What is before the committee at the present time is the amendment. What I am concerned about and should like to hear from members about, is whether, in their opinion, this would increase expenditures of the government.

While I do not agree with the purpose of the amendment, I would submit that it is in order. You, yourself, Mr. Chairman, quoted from page 4, section 3, (3), (b), which reads as follows:
. . . from its operations under this act during any crop year for which no provision is made in any other part of this act, shall be paid out of moneys provided by parliament.
It seems to me that we are not committing the government-
Order. Read the whole of it.
I did read the whole of it myself, before.
It says that losses, if any, sustained by the board-

Yes. I will read the whole of it.
(3) Losses, if any, sustained by the board
(a)	from its operations under part III of this act in relation to any pool period fixed thereunder, during such pool period, or
(b)	from its other operations under this act during any crop year, for which no provision is made in any other part of this act, shall be paid out of moneys provided by parliament.
It seems to me that at the time the losses were apparent parliament would be called upon to make the provision and that parliament at that time would decide whether any money should be paid out. Consequently this house, by adopting the amendment made by the leader of the opposition, is not committing the government to any payment whatsoever. We are simply providing that these losses shall be paid out of moneys provided by parliament when the time comes to make up those losses. Consequently, although I say I agree that 1946 should be paid, I do not want to endanger the whole principle of this bill by supporting the amendment of the leader of the

opposition and I do not intend to support it. But I think the amendment is in order under the rules of the house.
You mean that 1945 should be paid?
Yes.

In your own words, Mr. Chairman, there are two matters before the committee. One is whether this amendment is in order or not and the other is the substance of the amendment. You have asked for the opinions of members of the committee as to whether it may involve the government in some expenditure beyond the moneys now held at the credit of the farmers of Canada.
That is right.

I suggest that if you wait until you get unanimity of opinion on that in this committee, you will wait for a long time; because one man may say it will result in some loss to the government, and another may say it will not. If you are seeking advice, I would suggest that you take the opinion of the Minister of Agriculture. He said that now SI .55 a bushel is being obtained from Britain and a large part of the remainder is being sold for S2 and S2.50 a bushel, and he suggested that even in 1948-49 the price will not be lower than SI.35. I suggest, therefore, in arriving at your decision, that you accept his judgment on that and agree that this will mean no loss to the taxpayers of Canada.
That is not what I said.
Let us have a decision. If we are out of order, let us have a declaration that we are out of order. If we are not, let us go ahead with the discussion.

I wish to speak on the question of order only. I do so with considerable diffidence, having regard, Mr. Chairman, to your long experience in the chair. But we must, first of all, examine this bill to see whether it is actually a money bill or not. This was not a money bill originally, although consent from the governor general was obtained. It is a bill which has to do with the marketing and the buying of wheat. I submit that its primary purpose is not that of a money bill. I should like to refer you-

Order. So far as hon. members have indicated, it will not increase expenditures. Without further debate I should like to put the amendment. It is moved by Mr. Bracken:

Canadian Wheat Board Act
That paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of section 20 be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"Any crop year prior to or subsequent to the first day of August, 1945."
All in favour of the amendment will please say "aye".

Mr. Chairman, if you have now ruled that this is in order and you are going to permit it to be debated and voted upon, I wish to answer some of the points that have been raised by previous speakers. I would remind1 you, sir, that before I moved this amendment I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce if he would let us know how much money the board now has from the sale of the 1943 crop, the 1944 crop and the 1945 crop. I ask that just as a matter of information; because whatever that amount is, this board has invested it at relatively low rates of interest, while the farmers who own the money are paying high rates of interest on any sums they may owe. I asked for that information; I should like to get it if it can be made available.
After I moved this amendment the hon. member for Melfort raised some objection. First of all, he said he wanted to get a parity price. Forget that name; call it anything you like. It is supposed to be a price that bears a fair relationship to the cost of growing this commodity. The hon. member says that is what he wants, but he says this policy of paying $1.35 over a period of five years will give some stability, and for that reason he is inclined to accept it. If stability is all we want, regardless of the level, then there may be some merit to his point. Everybody wants stability.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, the leader of the opposition is putting into my mouth words I did not use. That was not my position, nor has it been the position of this group. We have said all along that we wished participation certificates paid yearly on the basis of parity, determined for each year.
Well, I am glad to hear the hon. member say that.
We said it before.
That is exactly what we want, but you objected to my amendment.
Your amendment is a different thing entirely. There is no parity whatever included in your amendment.

My hon. friend says he wants parity prices, and hon. gentlemen over there have said the same thing. I have not
heard anyone in Canada deny that we should try to get prices for agricultural products that are fair in relation to their cost.
Your amendment does not have anything to do with that.

You will have your chance to talk all you wish about this amendment. The government now come along with a programme under which they say that for the next five years they are to give the farmers $1.35 a bushel. It is realized that they are holding back a good deal of money which has been received but has not been paid over to the farmers; and the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture are saying they cannot give any more than $1.35 because they might need the surplus they now hold to balance up any losses. Therefore today they are not guaranteeing any more than $1.35 over the next five years. My point is, that is not a fair price; that is not a parity price.
You don't know.
I do know.
How do you know?
I know it is not for this year.
We have still four years to go.

The minister can speak later if he wishes. My hon. friends to my left are objecting to this amendment, but let us look at this situation. Today a fair price is $1.55. I have not heard anyone deny that statement. I am not suggesting that this price should be fixed for all time to come. Costs change. Costs may go up, as they have been going up. They may go down. The price received should bear a relationship to changed conditions as to costs from time to time; make it yearly, or whatever you choose. The point is that on the argument of the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture they say they cannot afford to pay more than $1.35 over the five-year period; therefore they say they have to keep these surpluses to offset possible losses. That is all the farmers are sure of under this legislation-$1.35 a bushel. I ask the hon. member for Melfort if he is satisfied with that. I am not. This is not a policy of stabilized prices at fair levels. Suppose the fair level is $1.55. This is a floor price policy, at $1.35. If you are to have only floor prices, which are less than fair prices, you must let the farmer have anything above the advance price when he can get it, because for many years he will have to take less than a fair price under this very policy.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

If the government had a policy of paying fair prices now, that would be one thing,; but that is not the policy they have. Theirs is a policy of floor prices. If, arising out of the latter policy, the farmer is to get fair prices, then when the world price is high he must be allowed to have it, because all too often the world price will be low and he will, on the average, be getting less than a fair price.
I think I have dealt with the substance of the objection of the hon. member for Melfort and the hon. member for Humboldt. What I want, what we all want and what I think the government want is to try to find a price that will bear a fair relationship to costs, not for this year alone, not for next year, not even for four years, but for all time to come. The policy in this bill will not do it, even for the present. The government is now depending wholly upon an international agreement to return this $1.35. An international agreement with one country will not give stability of prices to farmers. When you come to make another agreement three years from now, the price may be down to $1. Are you going to be satisfied with an average price based upon world prices of around $1, when you come to make a new agreement? You know you are not. That is the main issue. The Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture say they cannot guarantee more than $1.35 under these conditions. That leaves the impression that this is all they think the whole policy is worth, and that is not good enough to give a square deal to agriculture.
In saying that, I am not speaking only for the agriculturist, because, while it would do him good to have fair prices, just as it does the labouring man good to be assured of a job at fair wages, I say as well that if the relative income of the agriculturist goes down the whole economy will be adversely affected. If the farmer is to be denied his present purchasing power, he cannot in future buy as much goods from the people who make them in Canada, and as a result such people cannot maintain high employment in this country. Whatever else may be said here, that is involved in the issue we are facing right now. Are we to accept a stabilized price at the level of only $1.35, or are we not? If the policy of the government were to pay a parity price now I would accept it and ask no more. But that is not their policy; theirs is only a floor price policy, and in order that this floor price policy may give fair prices over a long period of time you must allow the high prices of the good years to be paid the farmers because the low prices of the bad years have to be accepted by them as well. That is the issue, and that

is all there is to it. I am sure we are all indebted to the Minister of Agriculture for the outline he has given us of these developments over the years, but what I have stated is the basic principle at stake, and that is what we are voting on in this amendment.

If that were the principle involved in this amendment I do not think there would be any objection to it, from this corner of the house at least, and I doubt very much if there would be any objection from any corner of the house. But look at the amendment itself. It strikes out paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of section 20 and substitutes therefor this simple statement:
Any crop year prior to or subsequent to the first day of August, 1945.
It would then read:
20. Subject to section twenty-six of this act, in this part "pool period" means any crop year prior to or subsequent to the first day of August, 1945.
That is to say, it puts every year as a single pool year. It means that if the price is high, we will say in this year of 1946-47, every cent would be paid out and nothing would be left in the pool to meet any call that might be necessary to bring the price up to parity in future years. That is what this amendment means. My hon. friend says that he does not mean that, but if that is so let him draft something that means exactly what we all want it to mean. He should not ask us to vote for something which means something entirely different from that which he says it means.
Any interpretation placed upon this amendment must be that each year is to be regarded as a separate year, that everything that accrues in the year must be paid out by way of participation certificates. I am in agreement with my hon. friend who says that participation certificates should be paid in addition to th6 $1.35 to make up to parity when parity is arrived at, but I would prefer to forgo that rather than to sacrifice the principle of this bill and jeopardize the growers of this country during the next four years. That is exactly what would happen.
The leader of the opposition knows perfectly well what may happen two years from now. A few days ago, the Hon. Mr. Strachey said in Winnipeg that wheat might drop once again to a level where the British government could buy it like chaff as they did in 1931 or 1932. We want to safeguard these people back home who were penalized in those years from a recurrence of the condition under which they suffered at that time.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

I have only one question to ask the leader of the C.C.F. party who has just spoken. He has indicated that under this arrangement the government could not pay out any participation certificates year by year, because at the end of four years there might not be enough money to pay the $1.35 average. My question is, is he satisfied under those conditions to take $1.35 a bushel as a complete payment for the crops of the next five years? That is what his whole argument leads up to.

I am not prepared to take $1.35. I would say that if the price of wheat remains high over that period the farmer's of Canada will not be asked to take $1.35; they will get the balance.
