I directed some questions to the Minister of Trade and Commerce and I wonder if he could answer them.
Did those questions have reference to the amount of cash on hand?
I asked how much money the wheat board held as a result of the 1943 operations, as a result of the 1944 operations and as a result of the 1945 operations.

I have not the figures showing the amount of money that we have on hand as a result of the 1943 operations, but every dollar of that has to be paid out in participation certificates. I have not the figures as to what cash is being held for the 1944 crop year, but again all that has to be paid out to the producers of the wheat.
That is entirely beside the point. I only asked for the amounts that were on hand.
I have not the amounts.
Could the minister not get that information?

I have been making an effort to get the information for the last hour. I find that I cannot readily get it and that it will require some time to make the breakdown. There is also the matter of whether or not the information should be made public.
Will the minister give us that information when he can get it? I am not asking him to do the impossible today.
I shall certainly be glad to do that as far as the 1943 crop is concerned and as far as the 1944 crop is concerned.
Will the minister also give us the average interest earnings on the balances held by the government?
I will try to get that information.

Will one of the spokesmen for the government clarify the position with regard to clause (a) which reads:
(a) buy all wheat produced in the designated area, offered by a producer for sale and delivery to the board at an elevator or in a railway car in accordance with the provisions of this act and the regulations and the orders of the board.
There has been a good deal of confusion regarding government policy. The hon. member for Battle River quoted from the "Wheat Pool Budget" which reported a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture. This is to be found on page 629 of Hansard, and I quote:
The Canadian government, through the wheat board, will take all deliveries of wheat up to July 31, 1950. This statement was made by Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, while addressing the annual convention of the United Farmers of Alberta, in replying to a question from one of the audience.
The Minister of Agriculture really did not make the position clear when he said, and I quote:
The statement which has just been read corrects what was said all over western Canada. It was said all over western Canada that, under the order in council as it was, there could not be more than fourteen bushels to the acre delivered. A member in that meeting got up and asked for a correction of that, and I corrected it much in the words of this report, which was not submitted to me before it was printed but which, nevertheless, to all intents and purposes does give the explanation which was given.
In discussing this point the other day, the Minister of Trade and Commerce made it clear that it is not the intention of the government to be committed for more than fourteen bushels per acre on 22,000,000 acres. When the minister suggested the other day that he would be prepared to withdraw this clause which we discussed at such length last night it was the understanding of those who heard him that it would be withdrawn and that an undertaking would be given by the government to make good the promise made by the Minister of Agriculture. I wonder if we might have some statement as to whether the cabinet ministers have been able to get together on this problem and whether the Minister of Agriculture, if he was correctly reported, was speaking for the government

Canadian Wheat Board Act

when he spoke in the west? I know the Minister of Agriculture does believe it will be possible to take this large quantity, but the minister has been wrong on some occasions, as he admitted a few days ago.
Occasionally, yes.
I think that, before we leave this section, the members of the cabinet should make clear just what the government policy is.

If my hon. friend will read the statement again he will find that it states exactly what has been said here continually, that all the wheat delivered down to July 31, 1950, will be taken at $1.35 a bushel. But that is not the question that is in the minds of my hon. friends from Alberta.
Up to fourteen bushels an acre.

No; all of it delivered down to that time will be paid for at $1.35 a bushel. That statement was made in Calgary and it is correct. But that is not the question raised by my hon. friends from Alberta. They are worried about wheat that cannot be delivered if there is a big crop and the elevators are full. Any wheat that is delivered will be paid for at $1.35 a bushel. There can be no question about that. Section 21 states:
The board shall undertake the marketing of wheat produced in the designated area in interprovincial and export trade and for such purpose shall
(a) buy all wheat produced in the designated area, offered by a producer for sale and delivery to the board at an elevator or in a railway car in accordance with the provisions of this act and the regulations and the orders of the board.
That is in absolute accord with what I said in Calgary and what has been said everywhere. But the question raised by my hon. friends from Alberta I argued under the previous section is taken care of by the fact that this house has to reconsider this agreement before the end of the period, and if, for any reason, it may develop that there is some wheat somewhere that the Canadian farmer could not get taken into the elevator because of conditions over which he had no control, the question would then have to be decided [DOT]whether the government would provide some means of his getting that wheat into the elevator. That question was argued on section 20, and it is safeguarded by the fact that this agreement must again come before the house, and all the facts will be before it when the decision is to be made. If I were to argue that question now I would say that in my opinion-I know I cannot always be right, as

has been suggested-no difficulty will arise, but in case any difficulty does arise I cannot conceive of this house, with all the facts before it, dealing with it otherwise than as has been suggested by many members here.
My point is that, as the legislation now stands, the wheat growers are guaranteed acceptance of only fourteen bushels on the authorized acreage. Is that not correct?
I would rather see that provision taken out, myself.

If you took it out it wTould leave the matter to be decided by order in council, and the farmer would have no guarantee. Certainly those of us on this side of the house would like to have a minimum of fourteen bushels to the acre rather than no guarantee at all; but, as I understood the argument of the hon. member for Acadia and the hon. member for Battle River, they wanted the government to state whether all the wheat that can be grown can be sold at this price or whether the government is restricting its contract to fourteen bushels on the authorized acreage.

I will tell you why I
should like to see that provision out. It is that when we go back to western Canada we shall hear on every platform this argument about the fourteen bushels. We have heard it ever since that provision was in there. It has been argued all over western Canada that because fourteen bushels is in there, that is all we are going to take. That has never been the intention of the provision. It was put in there, as I said last night, as a means of controlling acreage, and it has been utilized for other purposes since. The committee can do whatever they see fit with regard to it. Personally I do not think the provision in section 17 means very much. I should like to see the committee go back to that section and decide whether to leave that provision in or take it out. If they take it out we shall get rid of a lot of the discussion that we shall otherwise have about that fourteen-bushels provision.
On the general question about which my hon. friends are concerned, I do not see how we can give them any further assurance than is contained in this section. This section says that we must take all the grain that is delivered to us. I presume that means so long as there is some place to put it, because nobody would ask us to take it unless there was a place where it could be taken care of properly.

Canadian Wheat Board Act

Provided that the grain
grower is allowed to deliver it under section 17, under paragraphs (f) and (g) of which the board can refuse delivery to the farmer. Now, if the farmer cannot deliver it, the board cannot buy it.

I am sure that the
hon. member does not really think the board would try to stop the farmers from delivering wheat. The fourteen-bushels provision applies, not only at the end of the year, but right through, and that provision is put there for only one purpose. It simply says to the farmers:	You are all going to be given a
fair chance to deliver your grain. If you have a big crop it may have to be put under quota, even in 1947, not in 1949. But the bill says that, under any circumstances, that quota will not be less than fourteen bushels to the acre. That is all that has been said. But whether the provision is left in or taken out, the wheat board will be taking all the wheat they can possibly get just as fast as they can market it because people are starving for the want of it. So that the board are going to be pushing this wheat out to market as fast as they can get it out.

The Minister of Agriculture says that parliament in 1950 will be able to decide this issue. But the farmers are being asked to make a sacrifice today in taking less than the market price, and in view of that sacrifice they should have the assurance that they will not have to wait until 1950 for that decision to be made. The minister said yesterday, as reported at page 884 of Hansard:
I do not think any piece of legislation can be one-sided and when you say that the government must do a certain thing, there are some people who must see to it as well that the funds which the government is handling are protected.
It seems to me definitely that the minister is taking the weaker side. The argument on the other side is far stronger, because you are today compelling the farmer to take a considerable loss as compared with the world market price, a loss that may run anywhere up to ninety cents a bushel, and he is being given no definite guarantee that he will be able to dispose of all the wheat which he produces up to July 31, 1950, at a price of $1.35. That assurance should be given now. *The farmer should not have to wait until 1950 for it. It is true that section 21 sa3's:
The board shall undertake the marketing of wheat produced in the designated area in interprovincial and export trade and for such purpose shall
(a) buy all wheat produced in the designated area offered by a producer for sale and delivery to the board at an elevator or in a railway car in accordance with the provisions of this act and the regulations and the orders of the board.

The amount of wheat delivered will depend on the action of the board. The minister must admit that, if in 1949 the elevators become seriously congested, a quota will be put on deliveries and those quotas might not be lifted by July 31, 1950, in which case the farmer would not be able to deliver all his grain. The result would be that on July 31, 1950, there would be a certain amount of grain left in the farmer's bins, as to which he is given no guarantee at all. The minister says we can deal with that in 1950. Why wait until 1950 to say that the intention of the government is that the SI.35 shall apply to all wheat delivered to elevators and also to wheat left in the farmer's bins owing to the elevators being full?
I shall quote what the Minister of Trade and Commerce said as reported at page 855 of Hansard. I wish to congratulate the Minister of Trade and Commerce on the fact that he is the only minister of the three who has put this question fairly before the committee so that we can actually determine what the policy of the government is to be. Had it not been for the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce I, and, I think, other hon. members, would have jumped to the conclusion that the government was going to pay $1.35 a bushel for all wheat offered for sale by the farmers prior to July 31, 1950. The minister has made it quite clear that that is not so. Let me quote what he said.
No.

I shall quote what was said and then the minister may argue whether it means that or not.
As reported at page 855 of Hansard the Minister of Justice referred to a certain situation which might develop, and he used these words:
For instance, if you had an enormous crop the last year at frightfully low prices-
The minister contemplates that we might have that situation. The report continues:
-that would upset your calculations tremendously, as the hon. gentleman can understand.
Then I interjected the following:
Perhaps the minister would go a step farther. He said that we might have a tremendous crop in the last year, and in that case no doubt the elevators would be plugged. Would the Minister of Trade and Commerce still propose to accept for delivery, in that case, the grain that could not be taken by the elevators by July 31, 1950?
Then the Minister of Trade and Commerce
replied:
According to the statement I made, we propose to take all the wheat for which we can find space. We will take all the wheat produced to the extent of the available elevator capacity.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

In other words, if we have a very heavy crop in 1949 and it is not possible to take delivery of all that wheat, the government is not committed to pay $1.35 for that portion of the crop which is still left in the farmers' bins; therefore it is not true to say that the government proposes to take all wheat offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950, at the price of $1.35. It was for that reason that I offered the amendment to subsection 2, to make it quite clear that the government would buy all wheat at $1.35 up to July 31, 1950.
When we turn to section 17, paragraphs (f) and (g), we find the following:
(f)	fix, from time to time quotas of each kind of grain that may be delivered by producers to elevators or railway cars, witbin any period or periods, either generally or in specified areas or at specified delivery points or otherwise;
(g)	notwithstanding anything in this part, prohibit the delivery into or receipt by an elevator of, any kind of grain, or any grade or quality thereof, either generally or otherwise.
I do not think for one moment that the board would use these sections if it could avoid doing so; but, on the other hand, if you had a situation such as the Minister of Justice suggests may develop, then I do not doubt for one minute that they would be forced to use the sections, with the result that, by July 31, 1950, all wheat would not have been delivered, and that portion of it which was left in the farmers' bins would not be marketed at $1.35 unless, as the Minister of Agriculture says, the price in 1950 were $1.48. But if the situation was as the Minister of Justice suggests, an enormous crop at ruinously low prices, then the farmers certainly would not get $1.46 in 1950, and therefore they would suffer a loss on that portion of the wheat which was left in their bins. It is for that reason that I object to the removal [DOT]of subsection 2 of section 17 because it does give a limited amount of protection. It gives a guarantee that the government will accept at least fourteen bushels to the acre. If you take that out you are removing even the small amount of protection which the farmer has in this bill. Therefore I suggest that the government could very well have accepted the amendment which I suggested to the effect that, notwithstanding anything contained in the act, the government would agree to accept all wheat offered for sale prior to July 31, 1950. I know I cannot move the amendment; it has been ruled out of order. I am suggesting that the government should accept the suggestion.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce may say, how can we take delivery of wheat when there is no room in the elevators? Am I to

understand that, so far as the government are concerned, the only reason they are not prepared to give that guarantee is that they would have nowhere to put the wheat?
I think I can say that the government contemplates taking every bushel the farmers raise and offer for sale to the capacity of the elevators.
That is no good.
May I say this, and I am saying it kindly. The hon. member anticipates bad faith on the part of the people handling this legislation.
I am accepting the statement at its face value.
Again I repeat, we contemplate taking all the grain that is offered for sale to the full extent of our storage and elevator capacity.
That is not good enough.

Just a moment.
Further than that, if some situation does develop in which there is a large surplus, but which I think is impossible, I do not think, and I am sure that no hon. member from western Canada who makes a study of the storage facilities, and in view' of our wheat agreements and the demands of other countries for our wheat, thinks the situation which is expected by the hon. member for Acadia will ever come about.
Then the minister should have no hesitation in giving the guarantee.
I do not think it will ever occur. I do not think it could occur when one takes into consideration our elevator facilities, our wheat contracts and the demand for our wheat.
Put it in the contract and save all the argument.

If that situation does occur there is only one way it can be dealt with, and that will be done in the light of the conditions as they are at that time. I do not think it is practical to attempt to make any regulations or promises regarding these circumstances which I do not believe will ever come about.
The farmers of eastern Canada will consider that the government has now gone quite far enough, not knowing what the world economic conditions may be in 1950.

I wish to ask the minister a question in connection with interprovincial

, Canadian Wheat Board Act
marketing control. What is the position of a British Columbia farmer who owns an Alberta farm, grows grain on the Alberta farm and wants to take it to British Columbia to feed on his British Columbia farm?
The farmer in question can get the necessary permission by applying to the Canadian wheat board.

The arguments
advanced thus far by the ministers have not convinced me.
They have convinced me.

All through southern Alberta the farmers have almost a complex by reason of the fact that, during the war when it appeared there would be the greatest need for grain, in many cases they had to build makeshift retainers and containers on their land by using straw, wire and posts. Many of them have lost heavily because they had vast quantities of wheat piled on the ground, open to the weather.
They started out with tremendous surpluses of wheat in the elevators.

That sort of surplus may again develop. The reports which I get and which, of course, may not be by any means adequate when compared with those to which the minister has access, indicate that the countries in Europe which have been accustomed to producing wheat are rapidly returning to the production of wheat.
All the countries in the world such as Australia, United States, South Africa and others, which have been producing wheat are rapidly returning to a full production of wheat. What grounds have we, according to ordinary logic, in assuming that there will not again develop in Canada a surplus of wheat, provided that we have large crops? Those considerations are serious. You can find them in every reputable journal, in the words of everyone who is competent to offer an opinion. I think the time has come for the country to face up to a situation such as the one I am going to indicate. There is no doubt that we should get to the point where we can have a sort of ever-normal granary. That was the expression that the late President Roosevelt used. I believe it would be a good thing to have an ever-normal storehouse or larder. I consider that the government would be sound in adopting a policy something like this.
Let the government say: "We will accept all the grain that can be delivered in the elevator space we possess and we will go even farther than that. If the elevator space should
be found to be inadequate we will advance, either directly ourselves or through the province and then through the municipality, money to farmers with which they can build granaries on their farms, probably along the fence line. Those granaries will be built according to certain specifications which will guarantee that they will take care of the grain in good condition. We will allow the farmers to store their grain in these bins and the grain will be paid for in whole or in part, and will be the property of the dominion government, or the provincial or the municipal government as the case may be,, and on the grain, storage will be paid the farmers as though the grain were in elevators. Then we shall have the grain right on the farm, right out in the country where we can get it in the event of a crop failure or in an emergency which might make it necessary that people in a given area, in central Saskatchewan let us say, should have access to grain and other commodities which they need, without having to have them shipped from long distances such as Port Arthur at ruinously high rates."
There is nothing unsound in that proposal. It is the barest kind of prudence to have on hand in this country great quantities of the necessities of life. I do not wish to labour the dangers which we are facing by reason of new war weapons which might easily destroy our communication systems or the great storage facilities. I do not need to refer to these possibilities to impress upon everyone in this country the necessity of having grain stored right near the people where it will be needed. That, I should think, would be an argument in favour of the government adopting a broad policy under which it would assist in the storage of grain on the farms. If this policy were adopted the government could easily make the commitment which this group suggests that it make, and it could do so without any danger whatsoever of embarrassment.
Mr. IsICHOLSON: I do not think we are imposing an unreasonable demand on the taxpayers. An hon. member has intimated that people in eastern Canada would not be willing to go farther than the government has gone, but surely Canadian funds invested in wheat stored under proper conditions would be quite as safe as gold in the mines in the north or in the hills of Kentucky. If the Canadian government at this stage would give the assurance that they are prepared to enter into longterm agreements with our own producers, it would have a stabilizing effect on the people engaged in the industry in other parts of the world as well, and I do not think the Canadian government would be running any risk. But when we have a situation where the Minister

of Agriculture has publicly given the impression that the Canadian government will accept all wheat that may be produced in this period, and then the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce refuse to go farther than a commitment to accept fourteen bushels an acre on the authorized acreage, it is bound to have a disturbing influence on those who will produce in the next few years.
I wonder if the cabinet ministers can give some indication as to why they are worried, as to how many dollars they think might be involved if they gave the commitment that they would be financially responsible for accepting all wheat grown on the authorized acreage for this period.

As I said before, I do not know of any way in which even an estimate could be made at present. As a matter of fact, if the government were asked to give an estimate they would say that really there is nothing involved,-because we do not think this position will develop. On the other hand, if we attempted to put in a provision to safeguard that, we would have to try to safeguard the opposite position where the farmer does not wish to deliver and will not, when we want the wheat to send somewhere. We have discussed that fully with the persons interested, who handle the marketing of grain on behalf of the farmers to a larger extent than anyone else, and they are absolutely satisfied that everything is here that ought to be here.
They are satisfied with the fourteen bushels an acre?

They did not discuss that question; they discussed the question as to what will happen in 1950. They are absolutely satisfied that the provisions in sections 20 and 21 will take care of that situation, and for that reason I think the bill ought to be passed, so far as sections 20 and 21 are concerned, in its present form, and when we go back to section 17 the government has no strong views at all on that question. In its present form it would be acceptable, and it would be acceptable to take it out. But as to simply saying, why not put in this particular commitment, I do not think it is fair to ask the government to do that at the present time. I do not know whether I shall Be here in 1949 or 1950, but I can assure everyone who is here that, if I am here at that time, I shall be fighting as strongly as they will to see that proper provision is made for handling all the farmers' wheat for that five-year period, and I will tell the committee the reason.

On behalf of the government I have stated every year, since at least as far back as 1943, that the government is absolutely opposed during the transitional period to putting any limitations on the production of the farmers of Canada and the marketing of their commodity, and the reason we are opposed to that is that during the war we put on price control and, while doing so, we urged the farmer to produce as he had never produced before. We did so all through the war; he increased his production forty per cent, and we had a ceiling price on it all the time and held it down. Members of the official opposition or others are quite justified in saying that we did not let the farmer get all that he might have had for his farm products, as part of price control during that period. But we did not let others get all that they might have had. At any rate, they are quite right in saying that w'e did not allow the farmer to do so; but, since we asked him to produce to the limit, and held down his price, when we established floors under his returns during the transitional period we must be prepared to see that his whole product is marketed, whatever may be the amount he desires to produce; and if he goes ahead and produces, as he went ahead during the war and produced to the limit, then we must find a market for him at a level which is not lower than the floor. We passed legislation to take care of that floor. We did so in a different bill altogether.
I say frankly that in the legislation which I shall bring before the house-the resolution is on the order paper today-we are trying to see to it that the people who eat the food pay for it at floor price levels or higher. That is our effort. We are attempting to do that through agreements. We have sold the surplus of other products and we have sold a very large proportion of the surplus of this product at a set price. We say that we. are going to continue that policy just as long as we can in the transitional period and try to avoid having to take any money out of the treasury in order to take care of it. But we have on the statute books legislation under which, if the price does go down lower than that, we have made provision for taking care of it. This one is just the same as the others. We as a government are committed to the policy of taking the farmers' product. All we are suggesting at the moment is that we cannot see our way clear to putting into this statute that we are to do something on July 31, 1950, when we do not know what the circumstances will be. But this government, as a matter of policy, are

Canadian Wheat Board Act
oommitted to finding some way of dealing with any problem of export in 1950 in relation to farmers.
Will the minister tell me in what words and by whom is the government committed to this policy?

Any minister of this government who rises in his place in the house and presents a policy as a government policy commits the government to it. That is the government's policy on that particular matter. Every member of the government sat and listened to the policy being pronounced. It was decided in council first, brought here and presented to the house and stated over and over again. Hon. members on the other side of the house were urging us to accept the United States policy which is to set parity and then take ninety per cent of the production at parity. We said that we would not do that, that we would not cut off ten per cent but were going to take 100 per cent.
Does the minister believe that the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce up to the present time in this house have committed the government to accept all the grain which is offered for sale?

I say that the words of the government over the last five or six years, and spoken here in the house, have committed the government to take the total production of the farmers or to see that it is marketed at floor prices; and not only in our speeches but in the legislation we say that if we have to buy it at a stated price which is higher than the market price in order to maintain the floor, then we are going to buy it at that price and pay the difference.
If the government of the day committed the government during the last five or six years, why is the Minister of Trade and Commerce so hesitant to commit the government now in this debate?

I will answer that by asking another question. If the government is committed to that action as a matter of policy, why should a member of the house insist on our laying down now a method by which we are going to put it into effect four years hence when we do not know what the circumstances will be at that time? This government has been committed to that action as a matter of policy; but when you tell us to put into the act now that we are going to take delivery-if not in the elevator, on the
farm-of all the farmers' wheat on July 31, 1950 at SI.35 a bushel, we simply say that, without the facts before us. we do not know how that should be done. It is all very well to say that in the United States there is some kind of a granary that can be locked up, but we have not granaries of that kind here and we do not market grain here in the same way as they market it in the United States. With the circumstances as they are here, I think it would not only be wrong to put this provision in but that we would be putting into the act something that we probably could not carry out on July 31. 1950, under certain circumstances; and this house would not permit us to carry it out in any event if it were one of these circumstances which has been spoken of. There would be no safeguard in that if the house would not let us do it, and they would correct it if we made a mistake in doing it now.
Shall section 21 carry?

I will just say this for the sake of the committee and of the people of the country who will read Hansard. I am going to submit it to them whether the government, through the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Trade and Commerce or the Minister of Justice-the three ministers who have spoken in this debate-have committed the government to the policy of taking all the grain on the farm or anywhere else which is offered for delivery. They have not done that. There is not a doubt in the world about it. It is as clear as day. The Minister of Agriculture is as evasive as he can be in this.
No, I am not evasive.

It must be quite obvious to everybody. I just wish to answer one argument which the minister made. He expressed fear that the farmers might not be willing to deliver grain, we will say in 1949 or 1950. There is just one conceivable reason why the farmers would not be willing to deliver grain, and that would be that the world market price was higher than $1.35, and higher than $1.35 plus participation. If the world price at that time, we will say in 1949 or 1950, happened to be so much above $1.35, then certainly the government ought to be safe in raising the price to the farmer enough so that he will bring in all his wheat, so that the government could deliver it on the world market. I am really surprised-and I say it with all deference to the Minister of Agri-
Canadian Wheat Board Act

culture-that he would have endeavoured to evade this issue by using such a specious argument as he used this afternoon.

I am not using any specious argument. I am simply saying that the farm organizations are agreed that this legislation does safeguard them to the fullest extent. I am not battling for what we who are sitting here think. It is the opinion of farm organizations given to me no later than last night and today at noon.
Maybe you talked them into it. You are a good talker.
No, I did not talk them into it.

In section 21, paragraph (b), provision is made to pay to producers selling and delivering wheat, and so on. One question I wish to ask is in connection with the paragraph down to where it starts with "provided". Suppose a man sells his land or dies, say at the end of 1946. Under the first part of that paragraph (b), could he be paid what he was entitled to get on his participation certificates up to that time, or would such a person or his estate, as the case might be, have to wait until 1950? I come to my second question. There has been some talk today about making an interim payment. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar emphasized that it would be insisted on. How could you make an interim payment to anybody when you have not determined the full class who would participate in I960? For instance, there may be growers who grow only in 1945 and 1946. At the end of 1946 there may be that huge surplus about which we have been talking. It may be said that we should make an interim payment, but to whom would the interim payment be made? Would it be to the men who grew wheat in 1945 and 1946? At the same time there would probably be men growing wheat in 1947 and 1948 who would be entitled to participate in the very money being paid out, and the amount in which they would be entitled to participate by being future growers would not yet be determined; yet you are dealing with their money. I ask how you can do that. You are either going to pay it out in 1950, or you are not going to pay it out at all. Is that not the situation?

With reference to the first question dealing with the producer who has delivered grain and who dies in any year before the final amount of the pool payment is established, his executor will have to wait until the end of the pool term to get the participation. With regard to the second question, there are in this bill no provisions for interim payment.
There has been some discussion about it; and can the minister figure out any legal way in which an interim payment can be made before 1950?
Just offhand, and giving my own opinion, I think it would be very difficult.
It would be illegal, would it not?

Yesterday I asked the minister a question because I was quite concerned about certain compulsory features of the bill. Now the comments of the hon. member for Lethbridge have again raised that doubt in my mind. Yesterday I asked the minister if this was the only medium through which the farmer could market the grain designated in the bill: wheat, oats, barley and flax. The minister's reply was that it must go only to the Canadian wheat board for interprovincial or export sale. Now, in order to get this clear in my own mind, do I understand that a farmer can sell his wheat to a miller in the province in which it is grown, or sell his oats or his barley without restriction on his right of free sale, except when it moves out of the province or out of the country?
That is correct; he can sell to a miller or to anyone else within his own province, subject to the quota.

I wish to be clear on this one point, something along the line of the matter raised by the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. I have in mind the case of a man who had a considerable acreage of wheat in 1945 and 1946. He does not now like this pooling system, and wants to change his plan of operation. He will be in this pool for the first two years, during which he has produced a great deal of wheat, and during a time when the price was high. I suppose he will have to wait for final payment until 1950, in spite of the fact that he is not now growing wheat, and will have to take his loss along with the man who remains in the pool for the five-year period, by which time the price may be down to SI. Is that correct, that no settlement can be made in a case of this kind, and that a man must take his loss in spite of the fact that he has changed his plan of operation?
Long before that time he will find he is vrrong and go back to wheat.
As a member of the pool he will have to wait.

I think the government
is making a grave mistake in not complying with the wishes of hon. members on this side

Canadian Wheat Board Act
of the house in this regard. It seems to me that when the ministers are so firmly convinced that a situation such as we have been indicating will never arise, then to satisfy the country as a whole and certainly to satisfy the farmers they should place in this section an undertaking that the government will accept all the grain produced and offered for sale. On. several occasions the minister has pointed out that there will be ample storage space as at July 31, 1950, but he overlooks the fact that already some of the annexes that were built in the west during the war have been torn down and a great many others are being offered for sale by the elevator companies, who are calling for tenders on them. Nothing is clearer than the fact that gradually these annexes will be torn down over the years, so that the storage space available will become less and less. As time goes on, we shall have less room for storage. It is pure, unadulterated nonsense to say that the government's policy is to take all the wheat, when they have made it clear in this act that they have no intention of taking more wheat than they have storage for. Merely to say that they will have the storage or that they will be able to take all the grain that will be produced because there will be storage is certainly not a good argument. It does not seem to me that in their policy the government have committed themselves to take all the wheat produced. The Minister of Agriculture went to some lengths to say that this was the policy. If it was and is the policy, and if, as far as the government can see, there is no danger of a shortage of storage space, then surely it is only good business to put that in the contract. Whoever heard of drawing up a contract and leaving something to be written in at the end of a four or five-year period. No business concern would do that.
Today the farmers are taking for their wheat a price which is less than the world market price. That difference is substantial, running to about $100,000,000 a year. That is a tremendous amount of money, but the farmers are accepting that loss on the assurance that they will be given a guaranteed price for a period of years on whatever amount of wheat they produce; yet the government persists in saying that they will take only that grain for which they have storage. In the interim the storage facilities are being reduced. That is not good business. I do not believe the government should place the members on this side of the house in the position of having to vote against this section for that reason. The government have said they do not anticipate
any trouble over storage in the future. Then why not insert that provision, and let us get on with the business of the house?
Because it is not possible to foresee the circumstances that may exist.

Why not? You have assured us there will not be any shortage of storage space. Either the government are not convinced of the truth of what they are saying, or their policy is different. There can be no other interpretation of the statement just made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce. They do not believe the statement they are trying to convince us is true. If they did they would have no hesitation in placing that provision in this bill. The Minister of Agriculture says the farm organization is satisfied. Well, I know the minister is one of the best orators in Canada. There are times when he can almost make you believe black is white, and this is one of those occasions. But some of us in this house have gone over this bill very carefully. We are trying to be reasonable about it.
And we have heard the minister before.

He has been talking to a group of farmers, and I am afraid, when the members of this agriculture committee go home, they will become wise to what is going on.

Section 21, subsection 1, paragraph (d), gives the board the power to pay a further ten cents a bushel on the 1945-46 crop. In view of the representations that have been made by various organizations with regard to the 1945-46 crop, I wonder if the government would not withdraw this clause and substitute a clause that would allow them to pay out a greater amount of the proceeds from the 1945-46 crop. I think that should be done because a large reserve of money is being held by the board at this present time. The government might well give consideration to this matter in order to meet the demands that some of this money now being held shall be paid out to assist the farmers, instead of its being held for the five full years. I think this could be done without injuring the government's position in any way.
Canadian Wheat Board Act

I cannot see any valid reason for the 1945 crop being included in the five-year pool. Some of the ministers have been talking about the huge amount of money they are going to have. If that is so, we should get rid of some of it and pass it on to the proper owners. There are other things in connection with this that many of us do not like. It was suggested this afternoon that the eastern farmers think the government has gone far enough. That sentence was not finished; it should read, "has gone far enough in skinning the western farmer."
Some people do not realize that the western farmers have been subsidizing all the consumers of Canada in connection with wheat used in bread which all of us eat. A number of people do not realize also that we have been subsidizing the consumers of the world, because not very long ago the government through the wheat board, placed a ceiling of $1.55 a bushel on all wheat for export. That was done at the expense of the farmer.
When the Minister of Agriculture told us that this is a one-sided agreement he did not lay any stress upon the fact that that was because the cards were stacked against the farmer. I think a number of these matters should be taken into consideration in dealing further with this agreement. I realize that this is a long-term programme, but if we have to sacrifice millions of dollars in the price it is not as advantageous as some people would have us believe.

Subsection 2 of section 21 reads:
The board shall, if directed by regulation, pay to each producer at the time of delivery of wheat to the board, in addition to any other payment authorized by this section, a sum per bushel on account of storage of the said wheat on the producer's farm, for such period of storage as the board in its sole discretion shall fix for the purposes of such storage payment, which sum, however, shall not in any case exceed the amount payable for storage in a country elevator for the same period according to the country elevator tariff rate filed with the board of grain commissioners.
The question was raised that there might be a possible shortage of storage for the 1949 crop. The minister has said that they will only take wheat for which the elevators have space. What is the purpose of putting in that subsection?
The government may be faced with a situation where they may wish to pay storage on wheat on the producer's farm and we are asking for authority to do that.
In case the elevators are filled up or something?
And for other reasons.
What other reasons?

One was advocated from the hon. member's section, I think by the hon. member for Melfort; that is, the establishment of an ever-normal granary on the farm. That is a project or plan of which I think highly myself, apart altogether from this bill. If the government in its good judgment believes that storage should be paid to a producer on the farm, then we would have the authority to do it if this section passes.

I am not arguing against it because I think it is a good thing. I believe the government is showing good judgment in making provision for the storage of grain on the farm, but it only goes to support what has been said from this side of the house, that the government should buy all the wheat offered for sale up to the end of July 31, 1850. They would have provision under this section whereby they could provide for storage on the farm if they so desired.
Why not give us credit for having done something that you have suggested should be done?
I will give you all the credit I can; I am only sorry I cannot give you credit for being a little bit more lenient and taking all the wheat and using farm storage for that purpose.
The government did that under regulation some years ago for one year only, and the amount paid for storage was graduated according to the time of delivery of the grain.
When the wheat was delivered1 we paid an increased amount.
You are taking the power here to do it if you want to do it, but you are not undertaking to do it?
No; there is no obligation.
Why should you not undertake to do it on the same basis as you did it for that one year. That was a fair basis and it was based originally on a suggestion made by a committee of this party.

We are taking the
power so that if we are confronted with a situation like that referred to, or with other situations, we can pay storage.

I agree with the government that this clause should be in the bill. I believe they should have the authority to pay

Canadian Wheat Board Act
storage, but I should like to see the words, "not in any ease exceed" in line 25 deleted and the word "equal" substituted therefor.
If the government are to pay storage on the farm they should pay at a rate equal to that being paid the country elevators. Unless there is some reason for it, I cannot understand why that should not be stated in the section.
This is the same clause as was used in the old act. I do not think it is an important matter because it is anticipated that we -would pay the same storage as to the elevators.

Why not say so? I expect that that is what they would do and I can see no reason why it should not be stated in the bill. It seems to me that we are arguing about something that we are both agreed upon, but there is some reluctance to state it in the bill. It is only common sense to *state what you intend. That would be much more satisfactory so far as the act itself is concerned, and so far as the grain growers and we in the opposition are concerned, because we are out to protect the grain growers' rights.

I move, Mr. Chairman, to strike out in line 25 of page 11 of the bill the words "not in any case exceed" and substitute therefor the word "equal," so that it will read:
. . . such storage payment, which sum, however, shall equal the amount payable for storage in a country elevator . . .
And so on.
Amendment agreed to.
Would the minister also strike out the words in line 18 on the same page, "if directed by regulation"?
No.

I wish to say a few words in support of what the hon. member for Mel-fort said about the 1945 crop. I see the minister smiling at hearing mention of that again. Many farmers during past years have been wrongfully accused of disregarding contracts, yet, as regards the 1945 crop, the farmers feel that they are on the other end of that kind of bargain because, when the 1945 crop was being harvested and delivered, it was the understanding that there was to be a one-year pool and that participation certificates would be issued on that basis. Like the hon. member for Melfort, I am also in favour of the longer period of time in a pool of this kind, but I submit that to go back and include the 1945 crop in the pool is to a great extent doing the very thing that many farmers have
been wrongfully accused of doing in years gone by, namely, disregarding a contract. Therefore I support the suggestion made by the hon. member for Melfort that the board should consider making a substantial payment on the 1945 crop.

I am not able to follow' the two hon. members who have just spoken on this question and asked that a substantial payment be made on the 1945 crop, because I do not see why they should not ask for a full settlement for that year. I agree with their arguments otherwise, and I am sure that the Minister of Justice will agree with me, although he may not say so, but I know his ideas on these matters. There is no doubt at all that this is retroactive legislation. The farmers who produced wheat that year fully expected that whatever profits were shown on that year's business would be distributed to them when the business of the year was completed, and not to do so is breaking a contract with them. I do not know why the farmer should be expected to take the word of the government seriously in the future, as the minister has argued, if justice is not to be done to them on the 1945 crop. The government refuses to write into the act what will be done in 1950 about delivery of grain, and I was surprised to hear the Minister of Agriculture argue as he did this afternoon. Even municipal corporations are guided by the statutes governing them, and it does not matter how well intentioned a member of the organization may be; it is what is written in the statute that counts if there is litigation. Good intentions count for nothing; it is what is written that counts. I am surprised that the 1945 crop has been included in the five-year pool. There should be a full settlement made for that year, and then establish the pool from that time on.
Section 5 (section 21) agreed to.
Section 5 (sections 22 and 23) agreed to.
On section 5 (section 24)-Form of certificates.

Subsection 2 provides that no certificate issued under this part shall be transferred or assigned. I agree with that. But I think some provision should be made for cases where the certificates are held bj vendors under agreements for sale or by mortgagees who have been paid in full. The minister will know that in the west agreements for sale are usually on a crop-payment plan, whereby the purchaser delivers a part of the crop against the purchase price. Mortgagees usually demand and get a collateral crop agreement, whereby the mortgagor delivers a portion of the crop to be applied against the
Canadian Wheat Board Act

mortgage. The certificates are issued to the mortgagee and vendor respectively. But it has happened that, when these agreements for sale and mortgages are paid in full, the vendor or mortgagee continues to hold the certificates which will at a later date become payable. Provision ought to be made in this section whereby a producer who is not the actual producer, such as the mortgagee or vendor, may, under regulations issued by the board, be entitled to transfer and assign those certificates back to the actual producer of the grain on whose behalf the certificate was issued. It may be that there is some regulation of the board which covers that, because subsection 2 says: "except as provided by regulation, no certificate . . . shall be transferred or assigned." If there is a regulation covering the point I have mentioned, well and good; if not, I have an amendment to offer.
If my hon. friend will look at section 24 (1) (c) he will see that the identical case he mentioned is covered.
Is there a regulation in force now whereby these certificates may be assigned to the actual producer?

There will be regulations covering that point.
Section 5 (section 24) agreed to.
Section 5 (sections 26 to 33 inclusive) agreed to.

I wish to make a slight objection on behalf of our party to subsection 4 of section 34. This subsection should be deleted in the interest of humanity, if for no other reason. It deprives a man of the right to have any sort of living. If he has a farm and commits an offence the board can suspend his right to deliver grain. I suggest to the minister for his consideration that that is going a little to the extreme. It is not the man who commits the offence who will suffer; it will be his wife and children. If he commits an offence, fine him; do not deprive him of his livelihood. I suggest, with deference, that the subsection should be deleted. It is not necessary for the enforcement of the provisions of the act.
Mr. A\ RIGHT: I should like to support the remarks of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie. This can be a serious matter to a farm family because their living may be affected. By this subsection you are taking away the right of a man to work and earn a 
living for his family. I do not think it is necessary. A fine is quite sufficient for the purposes.
Will the minister not consider deleting subsection 4 of section 34?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Of course I am not familiar with the trade or the practice, but I am informed that the object of this subsection is to prevent repetitions. It occurs to me that the object of the subsection would be carried out if it were changed in this way:
. . . where a producer is convicted of a second or subsequent offence there shall be a suspension.
I think that would be reasonable.

Under the set-up, the farmer is not permitted to deliver his wheat anywhere else. It must go to the board. This subsection would work a hardship on the farmer who was convicted of an offence. I would suggest that subsections 4 and 5 should be deleted from the section. It seems to be drastic legislation. The board are all-powerful and the grain cannot be delivered anywhere else.

I would suggest to the Minister of Justice that it would be much better if the fine were made higher on the second offence. If a man is suspended from making deliveries he will have to grow the grain anyway and he will not have any granary room. I do not believe this is a sound remedy for the condition that the board has in mind.
I am of the opinion that this subsection is wrong in principle. It imposes economic sanctions against a person after he has undergone the punishment which the law provides.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If the hon. gentlemen wilt permit me, may I say that we consent to the deletion of the subsections.
Subsections 4 and 5?

Has the minister a statement now with regard to the quota and the way in which it is determined? If so, he might put it on the record.
That is, the authorized acreage?
Yes.

In 1941-42 the board established an authorized acreage for each farm unit in the designated area. This acreage was established to provide an equitable basis for a restricted total marketing within any one crop year. The original basis was sixty-five per cent of the 1940 seeded acreage of each farm unit. In any one year acreages may not be normal. A producer might have an exceptionally large acreage of wheat or an exceptionally small acreage, depending upon his seeding plans for the year. This actually happened in 1940, and consequently the board was ready at all times to adjust authorized acreages of growers who were at a disadvantage as a result of the distribution of their acreages in 1940. In addition, new land has 
been coming into cultivation in the prairies each year and provision was made to establish authorized acreages for such farms. As a result of the long period of drought in southern Saskatchewan in the thirties, full recovery in wheat acreage had not been made by 1940 on a great many individual farms. This factor was taken into consideration by the board in subsequent revisions of authorized acreages.
The hon. member for Calgary East and afterwards the hon. member for Portage la Prairie, I believe, asked as to the cost of the quota department for 1945-46. That cost was $100,389.10 and was paid by the dominion government.
The second question was as to the cost of permit books. That was $4,097.70, and that amount is included in the sum I. have just given, paid by the dominion government. A total of 261,000 permit books of twelve pages were printed.

The minister's answer does not cover the point I raised. I knew all that he has told me. The point I raised was that today when a farmer applies for a quota there is a different formula used in determining his quota as between different parts of the provinces, different parts of western Canada. What I asked was as to the formulas that were being used at the present time by the board in determining the acreage in various sections of western Canada, because we are being approached quite often on that point by farmers who want to know what formulas the board uses in determining a man's acreage. A neighbour of mine has a section of land and his brother has a section in the southern part of the province. Both applied to have their quotas adjusted. They got entirely different results, and they want to know and, I think, we should know, what formula the board is using and the reason for applying these different formulas. I can see that a different formula should be used, and all I want to know is what formula is being used.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Consideration has been given to the hon. members' amendments. We feel we cannot accept them. The object of the amendments seems to be to make this board subject to suit in the provincial courts like an ordinary corporation instead of preserving its status as an agent of the crown for suit purposes. We have talked this matter over among ourselves, and we consider there are very good reasons why the Canadian wheat board should be clearly recognized as an agency of the crown and that actions against the Canadian wheat board should be by petition of right in the exchequer court.
I do not want to get into a long, hairsplitting, legal discussion if I can avoid it, particularly since in some respects the law may not be entirely clear. But, as the act now stands, there is no doubt that amounts to farmers due on participation certificates cannot be attached for debt, and that is the way we want it to be for reasons which we think are good. If we were to accept the hon. gentlemen's amendments I think we would just have to put in a special section protecting these payments against garnishee proceedings, which could be done with some little trouble. But, as the act stands now, that is not necessary. There is no doubt that they are exempt from garnishee proceedings.
As the act stands now, on the state of the decisions in Canada, actions to be brought against the board must be brought in the exchequer court. As to the type of action that may be brought against this board it might be for an accounting; and if actions for accounting, based upon small claims particularly, are brought in the various provinces- one action in Alberta, another action in Saskatchewan and another in Manitoba, for example-at different times, two things occur. In the first place, the inconvenience to the board is extreme to the point where the operations of the board might be seriously dislocated; whereas, if an action is brought in one court, particularly if more than one action is brought and these actions were consolidated in one court such as the exchequer court, the
dislocation is much less extreme; the litigant, if he wishes to go to the Supreme Court of Canada, gets there much faster, and there is not the danger of conflicting decisions from the courts of the various provinces. We have therefore come to the conclusion that there is a particularly good reason here why actions against the Canadian wheat board should be brought in the Exchequer Court of Canada instead of in the courts of the various provinces. As the act is now, we believe that to be the case.
There is a second reason why it is most important that actions be dealt with just as expeditiously as possible, and that there be unanimity and consistency in the decisions. If actions against the board, such as actions for accounting, are not dealt with expeditiously, distribution may be held up. The board conducts its affairs prudently. If an action is brought, based upon the claim that the amount of the participation should be nine and a quarter cents a bushel instead of nine cents a bushel, or something of that kind, the normal way for the board to act would be for it to cease distribution- although it might be about to distribute $60 million or $100 million or something like that-until that action is settled. Therefore the procedure against the board should be procedure which is likely to be most expeditious and which will minimize the danger of conflict between the courts in the various provinces.
Yesterday the hon. gentleman mentioned the question of torts. We think that the only torts which would likely arise would be possible cases of negligence, such as those arising out of the operation of motor cars by employees of the company or something of that kind. The exchequer court has jurisdiction over claims of that sort. If there are any other wrongs or torts, generally speaking-although I may not be 100 per cent correct in what I say-the crown is not liable but the servants of the crown are liable. That again, I think, should be enough opportunity. Altogether, we have come to the conclusion that we should make it clear in this bill that this agency is really an agency of the crown which should be proceeded against as such in the regular way in which actions are brought against agencies of the crown.

What the minister has
said is, I think, one of the disturbing features of this bill. The crown enters the field of commerce and in its transactions ceases to be subject to the ordinary rules which govern and control financial and commercial trans-

And in this regard there have been abuses. The point that I wish to accentuate at the moment is that, day by day, we are seeing our ordinary transactions, which in the past were governed by contract and controlled by the courts, lifted from the area in which they had play in the past and brought into a special jurisdiction which is always subject to the let and hindrance of some bureaucratic power. It is that thread of compulsion which runs through this whole bill which is repugnant to a person who believes in what some are pleased to call capitalism and what others are pleased to call private enterprise.
The other evening I heard the hon. member for Calgary West say that this bill had as its only excuse a bad contract which had been entered into by the government in power, and that we must honour that contract even though it was an unfortunate one, that we must subject ourselves to coercive measures in order that it be fulfilled. I admit that the undertaking to Britain must be carried out, however burdensome it may be, but there comes a time when good reasons to serve bad causes are a bit wearisome. I wish to make my position clear. I have very little sympathy with this type of legislation; I am opposed to it and, if it were fully and completely understood, I believe most of the people of my province would be opposed to it.
This denial of access to the courts, this doing away with the ordinary arbiter of trade and commerce and subjecting everything to the arbitrary wish of one man is a mistake. I admit that, as long as the minister who sits opposite is in office, it is unlikely that there will be any difficulty in getting a fiat, but the fact is that we are placing ourselves under a yoke. I dislike a yoke, it is high time to free ourselves from this type of restriction, this type of yoke, and this type of socialism.

I am not so much concerned with my amendment to subsection 1, because I believe the trend of decisions in England at the present time is toward giving full effect to the express words of the action, so that it probably does not make very much difference. Also in all probability my amendment is out of order, since subsection 1 is not before the committee. As far as my other amendment is concerned, however, I wish to direct attention to the fact that the courts have stated that simply creating a corporation is not sufficiently explicit to give it all the attributes of a corporation if it is the crown that happens to be the corporation. How can any court forget that fact when it is brought out in the very next subsection? After saying it is a corporation which can sue and be sued, the next clause to meet the eye of the court states that for all purposes the board is an agent of His Majesty in the right of Canada and that its powers under this act may be exercised by it only as an agent of His Majesty in the said right. That clause must have been put in for some reason. It was not put in, I assume, for the purpose of rendering nugatory the previous subsection, but I am afraid that will be the result. All I am asking is that there be included at the beginning of subsection 2 the words, "Subject to the provisions of subsection 1 of this section." That is to keep in force, notwithstanding these words in subsection 2 that we have before us now, the full force it was intended subsection 1 should have; and I cannot see any reason in the world why that should not be done.

I was unavoidably
absent on Monday when this bill was up for second reading and there are a few things I should like to say. First of all, I should like to say we have supported -the general principles of this bill and we hope it will work out to the benefit of both the producers and the people of Canada. There has been a tremendous amount of discussion during this debate as to the value of legislation of this description, particularly as to the value of the United Kingdom wheat agreement with which this bill has much to do. It seems that every attempt has been made by our hon friends to the right to undermine this act and to make it more difficult to understand the agreement. I can well understand that because, when the agreement with Great Britain was before us last August, we had a clear indication of their attitude. The leader of -the opposition, in speaking to the British agreement on August 15, 1946, at page 4822 of Hansard, said this:
It is a bad bargain also because it will create friction between Britain and Canada. If in two or three years from now the world price of wheat is low and Britain does not come through with a higher price to us than the world price then is, we shall feel that she has reneged on this agreement. On the other hand, if two or three years from now, when the world price of wheat may be low, we press Britain to pay ns more than the world price, she will feel that we are unreasonable. So I say that the proposal is altogether likely to create friction between this country and Britain.
And then on- the same -page, 4822, he said:
I predict that in two years time, or a little more, this agreement will blow up, when the advantages to Britain are gone -and when her own people will be wanting to get food at the world price, as they have always wanted to, and when the world price will probably be lower than it is now.

We said that this agreement has been interpreted as meaning that, because Britain now is allowed to purchase our wheat at forty or fifty cents, or more, below the world price, and that when they came to make another agreement for the 1948-1949 crop they would then pay more than the world price because of having got our wheat now at less than the world price. What I said was that if we did not then get more than the world price, Britain might be interpreted as reneging on this arrangement; also that if we expected considerably more than the world price, then we might be regarded there as being unreasonable. These results may still come if, in the later years, considerably more than the price is not obtained, provided that the world price is low.
Britain can carry out this agreement without increasing its price above the world price, because all they undertook to do under paragraph (b) of section 2 was as follows:
In determining the prices for these two crop years, 4948-49 and 1949-50, the United Kingdom government will have regard to any difference between the prices paid under this agreement in the 1946-47 and 4947-48 crop years and the world prices for wheat in the 1946-47 and 1947-48 crop years.
The British government "will have regard" to it. There is nothing in the agreement saying that they will make up at that time for the advantage which they have gained now. They will only have to "have regard" for it. It might be only a cent a bushel; it might be five cents. But at the present time they are getting an advantage of fifty cents and more per bushel.
If it was intended in 1948 and 1949 that Britain should make up for the advantage they are gaining now, it could have been put in the contract. It was not put there. Now, when these prices come to be adjusted, if an additional price approaching the advantage Britain now has is not put in, there will be some misunderstanding here. There might be

some feeling that Britain had not carried out what was represented to be the intent of this measure, but nothing specific was put in the bill. All they have undertaken to do is to "have regard" for the advantage now given; that is all. If it was meant that they should pay fifty cents a bushel or more, then, because they are getting an advantage of fifty cents a bushel or more now, it should have been put in the agreement and, then there could not have been any misunderstanding.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said that this bill could have been improved in certain particulars. Certainly it could. This government leaves the impression that it stands for parity prices, for fair prices. The policy of this bill will not give fair prices. The ministers themselves have admitted that farmers may not get more than $1.35 a bushel for the next five years. There is not a student of agriculture in this committee who will agree that that is a parity price or a fair price for these five years. It will not give stability on a parity level, or on a level which will assure a fair price to farmers for their wheat.
