subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) moved:
subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: That the order passed today respecting the resolution with regard to the purchase, sale and export of agricultural products be rescinded, and that the house go into committee of the whole on the said resolution this day.

Motion agreed to.
Mr. Gardiner thereupon moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the purchase, sale and export of of agricultural products, for the functions and powers of the minister, of commodity boards and of provincial marketing boards in relation thereto, for the employment of officers, clerks and employees necessary for the proper administration of the act and the payment of their expenses and remuneration out of moneys appropriated by parliament for such purpose, and for the creation of a special account in the consolidated revenue fund called the agricultural products account, and to provide further that expenditures, other than the administrative expenses [The Acting Chairman.]
above mentioned, shall be paid out of moneys appropriated by parliament or out of the agricultural products account.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
The resolution which has just been read is preceding a bill which I propose to submit for the consideration of the committee and the house; and I am1 doing it this evening because of the suggestion made this afternoon that the bill might be introduced before we returned to a discussion of the speech from the throne. I do not know exactly what is the desire of members who wished that to be done, but I would imagine that the main reason for the desire to have the resolution discussed in committee and, if possible, agreed to, would be for the purpose of having the bill itself submitted to members of the house. I understand that at least some of those with that desire in mind thought it would be somewhat delayed in getting into the hands of members of the house if we returned to a discussion of the speech from the throne on Monday and then did not get back to a discussion of this bill until a week or ten days hence. I can understand that being the desire of members of the committee and I can also understand it being the desire of others.
We have in the city of Ottawa at present a large delegation of representatives of farm organizations who came here from all across Canada for the purpose of presenting their point of view to the government of Canada on the question of introducing a marketing act at this particular session or at this time. I may state to the committee this evening that they made their presentation this morning and at the same time they presented a model bill which they hoped at some time, either at this session or at some other session, might be presented to this house. I recalled the fact that in 1939 and 1940, just at the beginning of the war, a similar delegation approached the government asking it to place on the statute books of Canada a marketing act which would supplement the acts which at that time had been placed on the statute books of a number of the provinces, more particularly British Columbia. Since that time, I believe marketing acts have been passed by all the provinces, and they have all made appeals to us to place on the statute books of Canada a marketing act which would be supplemental to the marketing acts of the provinces and would make provision in general terms for dealing with the interprovincial and international marketing of Canadian farm products, over which the provinces have no authority or control.

Agricultural Products
At the time that proposal was made, just at the beginning of the war, I suggested that I thought it would be necessary throughout the war period that any boards set up to handle the marketing of farm products should be under the control of the federal government and under the War Measures Act, and that any authority they might have during the war period should be under the War Measures Act. That suggestion was accepted at that time; and today, for the first time since then, we had a proposal that a marketing act be introduced. In making that proposal to the government, the representatives of the farm organizations read a resolution, the second clause of which was to the effect that what they desired to have done in a marketing act was to legalize a continuation of much that had been done throughout the war under the boards set up under the War Measures Act. I suggested to them this morning that there was on the order paper a resolution which might be discussed in the house today, and that the objective of the resolution and of the legislation based upon it would be to continue in effect the powers we had been given during the war under the War Measures Act, through the different orders in council.
The first of these orders in council is P.C. 2138, dated May 23, 1940, which is known as the dairy products regulations. That has been amended by order in council on five different occasions: by P.C. 143, of January 10, 1941; P.C. 515 of January 29, 1941; P.C. 1984 of March 23, 1941; P.C. 3197 of May 7, 1941, and P.C. 5827 of July 29, 1941. It is under those orders in council that we have been marketing cheese, canned milk and other products down to the present time, and it is suggested that the authority we were given to make contracts with Great Britain for the delivery of cheese, canned milk and other dairy products should be extended under the bill which will be presented if this resolution is adopted.
I am giving rather a full account of what is in the bill itself, because I understand I must have unanimous consent in order to present the bill and have it given first reading, and if that is permitted I should like to have as much information as possible before the committee. The second main order in council was P.C. 2520 dated April 15, 1941, the special products regulations, as amended by P.C. 4211 of June 17, 1941; P.C. 2164 of March 20, 1942, and P.C. 9158 of October 6, 1942. That original order, together with the amending orders, are the authority under which all agricultural products in connection with which we have contracts with Great 83166-59
Britain, such as beans, apples and other products of that kind, have been dealt with'. The other main order in council is P.C. 4187 dated June 3, 1943, known as the meat board regulations. If I had started at the beginning in relation to the meat board regulations I should have gone back to the fall of 1939. The first order in council we had giving authority to make contracts with Great Britain had to do with bacon. It was first passed merely as a regulation empowering us to make contracts for the sale of bacon to the British food mission.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: These are the orders in council under which these various boards were set up?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
Yes, the three main ones, as I shall explain in a moment; but the one I am- dealing with now really had its beginning back in 1939. In 1943, when we began to make contracts with Great Britain to deliver not only bacon but also beef, lamb and mutton, it was changed from a baoon board to a meat board. All the preceding orders in council were brought together in the order in council passed in 1943, called the meat board regulations. It is the principle contained in those three original orders, and the amending orders, which is contained in the legislation I propose to bring before the house, which gives us authority to continue to carry on the dairy regulations, the special products regulations, and the regulations with regard to the sale of meat. I should repeat that the special products regulations give us wide authority to make contracts in connection with all other farm products except dairy and meat products. I should explain to the committee, I think, that, in addition to dealing with the contracts already entered into, the special products order in council, and therefore the act based upon it, contemplates giving authority to the special products board to enter into new agreements. The only agreement we have in mind at the moment is in connection with apples. During the war we have been handling apples under special orders in council, which made provision for cash, payments to apple producers where losses otherwise would have been taken, outside the special products marketing regulations themselves. For some time now, negotiations have been going on between Great Britain and the apple producers, particularly those of the maritime provinces and British Columbia, for the marketing of apples to Great Britain under contract, and we had it in mind that those negotiations should continue, as they could continue under the special products regulations.



Agricultural Products
The only o-ther fact that I think I should place before the committee at the moment is with regard to the terms of the bill. Under the bill, authority is being asked for only twelve months or until sixty days after the beginning of the next session of parliament. We are prepared to bring this legislation back every session in order to report on what has taken place under the agreements and to get authority to proceed for another twelve months. I should like to say it is not anticipated that we would get any other result at the end of each session than the authority to continue to a conclusion the contracts which have been entered into for the delivery of bacon, cheese and other commodities of that kind to Great Britain over the period of years or the period of months which would carry us through to the end of 1948 in some cases and into 1949 in others.
As I say, the bill will terminate in a year or within sixty days after the house meets, but our intention is that in coming back we would in all probability get the support of the house at least to carry out the contracts whcih have been made. I should like to place myself in the hands of the committee to answer any questions that may be asked.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that the existing boards will be empowered only to carry out transactions connected with agreements which the government has entered into with other countries, or will this bill enable the boards to carry out other undertakings which they have taken on with regard to shipments out of one province into another province?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: The bill will cover interprovincial and international shipments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Not only connected with the agreement. It does provide authority to deal with interprovincial transactions.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Is there anything new in the legislation proposed by the bill? I ask that question in view of the representations made by members of the federation of agriculture who are here and who have been looking for some legislation apart from what is contained in the orders in council.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
I understand that the persons representing the farm organizations who are here, particularly those representing farmers who are interested in the sale of apples which is one of the big items that would be dealt with in the future, are concerned that we should have similar authority to that

which we had under the orders in council in order to delegate some of the authority to agents of the government. In the case of the apple producers, it would be the agency which has been handling apples throughout the war. Thus an agency of the producers would in all probability be given authority to carry out agreements which have already been discussed in order to make effective delivery of a product in much the same way as bacon and cheese has been delivered under the orders in council that have been in existence.
I should not like to be too definite in saying that the bill does not go outside the bounds of the orders in council. Necessarily the bill is general in character. It might be interpreted as giving more authority in connection with meat products than the meat order gives. It might be interpreted as giving more authority in connection with dairy products than the order with regard to dairy products gives. Perhaps the necessity for this is to be found in the fact that more authority would be required to be given in connection with the special products board than in connection with the other two, if organizations such as those which have been handling apples are to be empowered to do what the others have beexr doing under the other two orders.
Therefore I should not like to say that the bill does not give any other powers outside those contained in the orders. The intention is that, in effect, it will give the same authority to the government as the orders, but it is our intention, in applying that authority, to carry out the arrangements which were made during the war, particularly in connection with meat and dairy products, and to apply somewhat similar principles to the handling of these other products.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: The minister says that the powers may be somewhat different. Will power be conferred on the board whereby all farm products will be compelled to be sold to that organization, such as apples or meat or dairy products? Does the dairy products board intend to have everything marketed through the board?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
I doubt very much if any such authority would be given even if we had the power to give it under the act. We have never proceeded in that way. We have that authority under the orders in council but we have not proceeded in that way. Take bacon, as an illustration. We certainly have not handled anything like all the hogs which have been produced; we have handled only a smaller part of them. The packing plants which have always done the business have carried out all transactions. We have simply

Agricultural Products
directed the operations. Under our authority, we have sometimes compelled those who might not have fallen in with the general plan of the greater number to comply with the wishes of the greater number in the marketing of the product. You need to have pretty general powers in order to be able to do that.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: I understand that the meat board has power to take over sufficient meat to fill the contract with Great Britain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: They have the authority.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Is it intended that they shall exercise that authority? And will the other boards exercise similar authority under the bill?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
In 1941 the dairy board took all cheese, as the hon. member knows. In 1941 or 1942 we said that only fifty per cent of the hogs that had been delivered on to the Canadian market from the packing plants could be delivered in that year. We did those things during the war, but it is not anticipated that we shall do more than make certain that the Canadian market is fully supplied and that the surplus is taken off and sent to the markets to which we have agreed to send it.
The present position is that we have no agreements except those with Great Britain. Those agreements call for our sending all our surplus to Great Britain. We have attempted to put into figures what we think the quantity is that we shall be able to deliver and we do attempt to reach that figure. However, if it were impossible to do so without shorting this market to the extent of making our people go below their ration, we would probably hesitate to do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: I was going to bring up the question of rationing. Certain types of meat are rationed; butter is rationed and so are other products. Is it intended, under this bill, to continue rationing so that we can fill our contracts with Britain?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
I think that will be determined entirely as the people of Canada generally think it should be determined. Take butter as an example. While we have less butter than we had in 1945 and in 1946, we have more butter than we had prior to the war. There are some who think we ought to do away with rationing because we have more, but the purchasing power of our people is so much greater than it was at that time that we would probably create some hardship to our own people if we did away with rationing at the present time. I am not sure that we would not be able to do with less butter if we did not have rationing, because certain 83166-59J
people would buy butter in greater quantities and in all probablity there would be other developments which would result in many people not being able to get butter. Therefore a lower consumption might result than we have under rationing. But that question is apart from this altogether.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Did I understand the minister to say that the benefits derived under the orders in council in regard to apples were confined to the maritimes and British Columbia?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
No; the position was this. Prior to the war, Britain had been taking fifty per cent of all the apples produced in Canada. They had been taking eighty per cent of the apples from the maritime provinces and a very small quantity, not more than a few thousand barrels of apples, from Ontario. The reason was this: Ontario and Quebec have a market in central Canada for all the apples they produce. What we did in the first year of the war was to say that no one can ship apples into Ontario and Quebec except by permit and that no one could ship apples into the prairie provinces except British Columbia, except by permit. Then we said to the maritimes that we were prepared to pay for the canning and dehydrating of their apples; they proceeded to have their apples canned and dehydrated, and the government took them over and paid a price for them. The next year the whole procedure was changed and put in a different form of contract which has been followed from then down to the present, whereby we guarantee the apple producers in the maritimes and British Columbia certain returns on their apples. Then they proceeded to market their crop under the efficient marketing board which operates right across Canada. That board proceeded to carry out all the transactions in connection with marketing. The government had their records in connection with those transactions, which cost us a considerable amount of money each year, some $2,000,000 to $3,000,000 from the treasury of Canada. But they did no marketing by contract with any country outside Canada. They did, after the first year, sell some apples to Britain, and British Columbia in particular sold a considerable quantity of apples in the United States. They marketed the crop, generally speaking, right across the country and I think the results have been satisfactory. Ontario's main consideration was a guarantee of its own market in the central part of Canada. That arrangement worked out satisfactorily, and it was only when there was a scarcity that a permit was issued allowing apples to come in

Agricultural Products
from outside. Those apples came in under an arrangement with the apple growers of Ontario and Quebec.
The desire at the moment is to have a contract with Britain, and Britain is desirous of having a contract to take a very considerable quantity of apples, particularly from Nova Scotia and British Columbia, and to have them marketed there under agreement.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Will the legislation contain provisions continuing the embargo on our cattle going to the United States? If so, will any relaxation be made to permit at least of a token shipment of our cattle?

speechtext: The bill to provide for the sale and export of agricultural products has no provisions in it for the control of either exports or imports of any farm product; that is, control in the sense of limiting exports or imports. That comes under another bill, the export and import bill which is already before the house.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext: Do they take the recommendations of the Department of Agriculture?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE, SALE AND EXPORT-COMMODITY AND PROVINCIAL MARKETING BOARDS
speechtext:
Recommendations would be made by the department but they would be carried out under the other bill by the Department of Trade and Commerce. That is the machinery through which it has always been done, and the power for doing it will be taken in the export and import bill, not in this bill.
With regard to token shipments of cattle to the United States, I discussed that question with the ranchers and producers generally when I was in Calgary. Most of our cattle which have been going to the United States have gone from the western provinces, particularly from the ranches, and a considerable quantity have been going from western Ontario as well. We do not feel that there is any necessity for any token shipments to the United States, because we have a definite understanding with the United States that, at any time we desire to go back to the quota that we had prior to the war and down to 1942, that quota will be provided for us. There is no misunderstanding about that. That can take place any time we wish to have it take place. I would hesitate to go to the United States and suggest that in order to strengthen the understanding we already have with the United States government, we should ask them to take in a token shipment of, say, some fifty thousand cattle. I do not know exactly what we would do with them if we did send them there. There are many dealers in the United States who deal with ranchers and others on this side of the line, and how we

would divide up those cattle I do not know. But I am certain that there is no necessity for token shipments for the purpose of establishing our right to be in that market, for that right is already established both by correspondence and by personal discussions with the United States government.
But we are concerned about something else. In 1945 we shipped 573,000 head of cattle in cans and in frozen form to the United Kingdom and Europe, over 400,000 of those cattle going to Britain and some 100,000 odd going to Europe in cans, making a total of 573,000 head of cattle. We never had the right under the treaty we had with the United States to ship into that country more than 220,000 head of cattle, which included not only our quota but whatever number the Mexicans sent there. So that our quota actually amounted to 193,000 head. These were mostly top-grade beef. We never did have a good market in the United States for canners and cutters and lower grade beef. We could not do very1 much better in the United States on these than we can do at home. They wanted our high-grade beef.

I should like to thank the minister for the statement he has made. I know we have had a good market in Great Britain and, in fact, overseas generally for a considerable time, and are apt to have one for the next one or two years.
While the minister was in Calgary, I am quite sure that the live stock men there, particularly the ranchers, must have presented to him their fears that that market would fairly rapidly dry up and that we would be left in the position where we w'ere during the war when we were not economically able to compete with other parts of the world for the overseas market. The, only place that we could sell our surplus beef, particularly high-grade beef, was in the United States market.
As the minister knows, a considerable number of ranchers in southern Alberta have fairly close connections and contacts with cattlemen in the United States. As a result of talking with their friends across the border, they have become considerably disturbed at the change in the complexion of the United States congress particularly, and feel that there might rapidly be imposed, so far as the United States is concerned, an embargo against the importation of cattle from Canada into that country, particularly in view of the fact that during
the present period they have been short of beef. In fact there has been a great meat shortage in the United States, and we have not been sending any cattle to them.
I know that a considerable number of these men who have been in this business all their lives and know it well and who also know conditions in the United States-some of them have ranches in the United States and Canada -have been concerned that, unless we send what I spoke of a while ago as token shipments, we shall be in danger of having that market cut off altogether.
While I am quite happy about the market at the present time, it is the future that I am thinking of. Under the new regulations, I am wondering whether it would not be possible to do what the cattlemen of the west feel should be done, namely, to send shipments of some kind so that, as one of the biggest of these ranchers expressed it, we may be able to keep the ditches wet so far as imports into that country are concerned. I believe that these men know what they are talking about, and I am convinced that it would be in the interest of the country as a whole to follow along the lines which they suggest, to some extent at least. I should like the minister to comment on that point rather than on the markets that we have overseas at the present time.

The delegation from Britain which was here last week came here to discuss two things; one was meat and the other was wheat. The suggestion made was to the effect that they were desirous of getting meat from this country, and, in particular, beef was mentioned. They would like to get it in as great quantity as they are getting it now, and in greater quantity if possible. Naturally I raised the question which is in the mind of ranchers and others who are producing cattle across Canada. I asked how long were we likely to have a market in Great Britain of the same proportions as we have it now. The reply I received was that there would be a general shortage for a considerable time. They did mention a term of years. I hesitate to mention a term of years to the committee tonight, because I do not know that it was given to me with the idea of mentioning it or making them responsible for any particular figure; for, just as some say, that I guess wrong sometimes, I suppose ministers and governments elsewhere may also guess wrong sometimes.
In this case the minister and the others who were with him were insistent that for a considerable time, a longer time than we have considered in contracts with them for meat,
Agricultural Products

there would be a decided shortage, and they were anxious to make arrangements to get as great quantities as possible from this country over as much of that period as possible. For that reason I do not think that, in so far as numbers of cattle are concerned, there is any danger of the British and the European market drying up to an extent which would leave a surplus of cattle on this market in any reasonably long future period. I think it will extend for much longer than most of us had expected.
In so far as the United States market is concerned, it has been good for our cattle. They are prepared to take them but, as is generally known, there have been times when they have put fairly high duties on them.

The history of the matter is this. Back in 1942, after consulting with the Americans, we put an embargo on beef going into the United States, for the reason that we were taking so many hogs off this market, and had so many troops training that we were short of meat. We stopped beef going to the United States and it was all consumed here for about a year and a half. We did not send any to Britain. We sent bacon and ham to Britain, reducing our own supplies so far as hog meat was concerned, and we replenished it with beef. A year and a half later we would probably have considered taking the embargo off cattle going into the United States and, while considering the question, we had discussions with the Americans with regard to it. I myself went to Washington and discussed it with the secretary of agriculture of that time. As hon. members know, the Americans were then lease-lending beef to Britain. We were not lease-lending beef to Britain but we were sending, under mutual aid, bacon and other food. We sent no beef, and the Americans themselves made the suggestion that it would be misunderstood in the United States if we were to send cattle to that country while they were lease-lending to Britain. Their suggestion was that we might [DOT] send our cattle over under mutual aid direct. We acted upon that suggestion, and from that time to this we have been sending cattle to Britain, with the results I have indicated.

While the Americans themselves were short of beef, they wrote and asked us for permission to cancel for the time being that part of the quota which had been given to us and to permit of their giving it to Mexico or anyone else they could get meat from for the time being, and in writing at that time they gave us a definite undertaking that, whenever the situation was such at the end of the war or at any time-they did not specify the end of the war but any time the situation changed-that we were desirous of coming back into that market we would have the same quota as we had before.

I was pleased to hear what the minister said with regard to our present market in the United Kingdom and Europe, but there is the fear that it is only a temporary market. I am glad to hear the minister say that these people thought it would be a market for some-years longer than the term of the present contracts. I had an idea that it was a very temporary market in the United Kingdom and Europe, and that probably their natural market was the Argentine because they could buy greater numbers of cattle and have them transported reasonably from the Argentine, so that that would be their natural market rather than the market in Canada. I am quite satisfied that more and more we shall have to remove controls of that kind. I think it will be necessary
for a time to go along much as we were, but everyone anticipates that in due course we shall need to go back to taking what is surplus, over and above what is utilized, and fill our contracts with that, and we shall have to make our contracts conform to the quantity that we can obtain in that way.
I do not know how many members are familiar with the practice followed in Britain prior to the war. In 1932 they began to plan having meat conferences which took in all the nations that supplied meat to Britain, and they had a meat council which took in the nations within the British commonwealth that supplied meat to the United Kingdom. We came in the meat-council class, those within the empire who supplied meat to Britain; but, unfortunately, we were not able to take advantage of the situation in the manner in which most others were. We have a federated form of government under which we could not go to individuals and take live stock. Countries like Denmark could requisition their product, send it over and fill a contract for a stated amount and make sure they filled the contract to that amount. Britain in those years from 1932 down to the beginning of the war had definite undertakings from nations all over the world that they would supply a certain amount of meat to Britain. That is the only way in which she could be assured of her meat supply. When it came to Canada we had to say, "We are not in a position to say that we can ship you a certain amount because we have not the authority under our constitution to go and get it." Therefore Britain said, "We will give you an over-all quantity of 280,000,000 pounds of bacon." We were only supplying her about 160,000,000 to
200,000,000 pounds at the time. She said, "We will give you 280,000,000 pounds. We will be responsible for putting that quantity in and for saying to the other nations of the world that we will get that from Canada, and then take our quantities from the other countries." That is the method on which we proceeded until we got into the war. Then, under the War Measures Act, we took the authority which the other countries had prior to the war; that is, most of the countries other than those that were in the same position as ourselves, and I think maybe Australia was in much the same position. We then took the quantity which we undertook to deliver. We did that until about 1944. Then our people were very much concerned about not getting the kind of meat they wanted, when they wanted it and how they wanted it, and so we eased up on that. In easing up on it. we lowered the amounts we
Agricultural Products

said we could and would send to Britain, and those quantities in the contracts have gone down from that time, first down to 450,000,000 pounds and then down to 350,000,000 pounds, and now we are trying to turn them upward again in order to get more meat. We realize that the time will come when the authority we are taking in this act, which is a continuation of the authority we had under the orders in council, is something we are not going to have and therefore we may as well start to ease away from it and get to a basis where we know what we can supply by providing the surplus to Great Britain and they know in advance what we can supply.

What I should have said is that the tariff rate prior to the war was three cents a pound. Under the right which the president had, he could cut that rate to one and a half cent a pound; and he did cut it to one and a half cent under the agreement. Under the conditions which then existed, it was not very profitable, if profitable at all, to sell cattle into the United States under a three-cent duty, but it was profitable under a one and a half cent duty. The way the matter worked out was that in the first year I think we did send over the total number that we were entitled to send over, the 193,000 with the

special duty, but they all went over in a few months. Then the year was split up into four sections, and we took three months at a time and had a quota for each three months. The Americans asked for that because they did not want all the cattle dumped in there in a short time, then none coming in for a long time. My memory is that, after we provided for this dividing up of the year into three, there were not more than two years-and my memory is that there was only one-in which we reached
193,000.	That was not because we could not have sent more at three cents, but we did not have enough cattle; or at least we did not have enough of the quality required to send over and supply even the 193,000.

I say quite candidly that so far as I am concerned, and so far as the government is concerned, we realize that the natural market for high-grade cattle from Canada is the United States. We also realize that the natural market for quite a number of other things is the United States. But so long as we maintain our present ceiling levels in Canada and so long as the United States has her present price levels, there is not any possibility of opening up the boundary line. I am not arguing the question whether we are right or wrong in maintaining our present levels. It is and has been the policy up to the moment to maintain on everything a lower price level in this country than prevails in the United States. If we wish to maintain that price level it would be impossible for us to open up the boundary line on food products. We would just lose all our food products in a very short time and would) be on the higher level. That might be a good thing for the farmers in the end; I am not going to argue 83166-60

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I intended to make a very short statement about the business ahead. We had intended to have that statement made, before we received notice this morning of the intention of the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) to move the adjournment of the house to discuss a matter of urgent and definite public importance, but now it seems quite likely that discussion of that motion will take the whole of Monday.
As hon. members are aware, on Monday we automatically return to the terms of the resolution moved by the Prime Minister on January 30, dealing with the address. It was the intention of the government, I may say frankly, that we would finish the debate on the address by Thursday of next week; and if we are not able to do that, in view of the new developments, we certainly expect all cooperation possible to have it concluded with the utmost speed. We realize the position of those who moved motions of non-confidence in the administration, and that they should have an opportunity at the earliest possible date of obtaining the decision of the house on the question of confidence in the government. It must also be realized that the government itself will welcome the earliest possible decision on this question. While, however, we realize the responsibility of all parties in this regard, we realize that the government has a special responsibility in regard to emergency legislation and it intends, if necessary, by appropriate parliamentary procedure, to ensure that this legislation is not imperilled by any technicalities. If, therefore, Mr. Speaker, the debate on the address should show signs of being unduly prolonged it may be found necessary to renew motions such as those adopted previously this session for giving precedence to emergency legislation. If a further extension of time for emergency legislation should be necessary we have the assurance of the leaders of the various groups that they wall cooperate with us in this.
It is only fair to say that the attitude of all parties at the conferences held has been most helpful, and with the same cooperation we should hope for speedy disposal of the address and an early return to the consideration of the emergency legislation, making provision, with the cooperation of the house, for such extension of time as may be necessary.

With respect to the spirit of the remarks just made by the right hon. leader of the house I may say that we are in entire accord. I think it will be agreed by members of the government that those who

Peace Treaties
sit in opposition have been quite fair with the government in making possible the consideration of their emergency legislation before the debate on the address was concluded. However, it was felt that in view of these amendments to the motion the debate should not be longer delayed. I agree entirely that if the debate should be extended to any length the government must make its own decision as to what procedure it will adopt. We do not propose to embarrass the government if on any technical grounds they fail to have this emergency legislation dealt with by the end of March. We do not intend to embarrass them by taking advantage of any technical position such as that which might arise.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Will private members lose any of the days they would ordinarily have to discuss private members' resolutions because of the debates that have been carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I would think they would lose them unless provision is otherwise
made for special consideration later on in the session.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Will it mean that there will be no private members' resolutions discussed?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It will mean that a lot of time ordinarily used to deal with private members' resolutions will be lost. I think a discussion would have to be held in regard to making special provision for that.

What will be the procedure on Monday? Will there be a motion to adjourn the house, or is it the intention to take up the matter introduced by the hon. member for Peel on the address? If that is the intention, I shall protest because it is not the proper way to proceed.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I may be in error, but my conception of the rules is that a motion to adjourn the house to discuss a matter of urgent and definite public importance is made before the orders of the day are called and after routine proceedings. The order of the day next Monday would automatically be the special resolution which was passed unanimously by this house. If any hon. member gets the permission of the house he would be in order to move the adjournment of the house on a question of urgent public importance ahead of the discussion on the address.

At eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
